#3077. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.

#3076. Apple Brings Its iPhone Broadcasting to Formula 1 at the Las Vegas Grand Prix

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apple, the F1 broadcast provider in the US, is supplementing coverage with its own iPhone cameras.

When you watch a Formula 1 race on TV, the screen is packed with lap times, driver stats and real-time video from inside the cars and around the track. During the Las Vegas Grand Prix race, some of those views were captured with iPhone Pro phones and transmitted in real time over T-Mobile’s 5G network.

Using iPhone cameras for big events is no longer a novelty. Apple has been shooting its event videos and ad spots with iPhone Pro models outfitted with cinema-grade lenses, SSD storage and broadcasting gear for several years now. In May, Apple broadcast a Major League Soccer game shot with iPhones strapped to professional lenses, following it up with a Major League Baseball game in September using its own camera hardware,

But compared to a ballpark, F1 ratchets up the complexity, especially in Las Vegas. At the Las Vegas Grand Prix, the race track snakes 3.9 miles through the city’s downtown core. Its route includes the famed Strip (South Las Vegas Boulevard), where most of the big hotels are.

“We control everything on baseball, so we can do whatever we want there,” said Royce Dickerson, executive producer of live sports at Apple TV. “We did 14 iPhones on top of our normal camera complement” during the baseball broadcast. He noted that 10 of those were connected via T-Mobile’s 5G wireless network.

But integrating iPhone cameras into an F1 broadcast, even for the sport’s US broadcaster, is more of a challenge. “I’ve been doing TV production for 20-plus years,” said Dickerson, “and the scale of their operation is unlike anything I’ve seen before.”

Because F1 has agreements with other camera partners, Dickerson did not specify how many iPhones were set up around the track. Neither Apple nor T-Mobile explained where the iPhones were placed in order to capture the speedy F1 vehicles racing around the Vegas Strip. I suspect they were likely deployed in more conventional environments for smartphone cameras, like the team garages and roving to catch celebrities in the paddock area and in the stands, though the iPhone setups wirelessly broadcasting footage at earlier sporting events means they could be easily placed in many locations on and above the streets.

“You really have to work hard to earn the fans’ attention [and] that viewing experience,” said Dickerson. “How are you getting your fans closer to their favorite athlete, to their favorite driver, to their team, to the personalities that surround the sport?”

In the T-Mobile zone at the Sphere – an area sponsored by the carrier and open to T-Mobile customers – at least 10 iPhone cameras were used to cover a stage where concerts played between events. That number is based on a diagram shared during a tour of T-Mobile’s Tech Trailer, where the company’s event coordinators stay on top of things like crowd movements and line lengths.

Dean Locke, executive director of broadcast, media and race operations at Formula 1, sees the combination of multiple cameras streaming wirelessly over 5G as an essential component to the Las Vegas race.

“If we just did cameras at a low level, the fences and track, we haven’t done a very good job,” said Locke. “How can we open up stages, concerts and all of the activities? Each race has a real kind of personality to it. You can only [capture that personality] with huge amounts of cameras, huge amounts of technology.”

If Apple is using iPhones to record live sports, are they recording any of that footage using spatial video for viewing in the Vision Pro? Imagine getting a track-level view of a group of Formula 1 cars speeding past at 200 miles per hour with Apple’s depth effect. “[There’s] nothing at this time I can say about it,” said Dickerson.

Editors’ note: Jeff Carlson’s travel costs for the F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix were covered by T-Mobile. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

#3075. AppLovin vs. Magnite: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Two ad-tech stocks, one with explosive growth and sky-high margins, the other a conservative bet on connected TV, with very different balance sheets.

By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 12:56PM EST

The digital advertising landscape is evolving rapidly, forcing investors to choose between specialized platforms. Should you bet on AppLovin (APP +5.35%) or Magnite (MGNI +2.42%) for your long-term portfolio growth?

AppLovin focuses on high-performance mobile app marketing, while Magnite operates as a sell-side platform connecting publishers with advertisers across connected TV and digital audio. Both companies benefit from the shift toward programmatic advertising, where software automates the buying and selling of digital ad space to reach specific audiences more efficiently.

AppLovin provides a marketing platform designed to help businesses advertise and measure their performance, primarily within the mobile gaming sector. The company utilizes proprietary technology to power major mobile games and is currently expanding its reach into broader consumer brands. It maintains strategic relationships with major industry players like Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG), Meta Platforms, Amazon (AMZN +3.96%), and Unity Software (U +4.27%), though it often competes with these same entities.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, AppLovin's revenue reached $7.6 billion--a 57.8% increase year-over-year on a continuing operations basis (excluding the divested Apps business). Net income was $5.0 billion, yielding a 65.9% net margin (the share of sales kept as profit after all expenses).

As of December 2025, its current ratio was 3.3x (over three times more current assets than short-term liabilities) and its debt-to-equity ratio was 1.7x (total debt relative to shareholder equity). Full-year 2025 free cash flow reached $3.95 billion after operating costs and capital expenditures.

Magnite operates as an independent sell-side platform, helping digital publishers monetize their content across connected TV, online video, and mobile displays. By serving as a bridge between media owners and ad buyers, the company facilitates ad placements in approximately 190 countries worldwide. It has established key partnerships with organizations like LG Ad Solutions and recently began working with OpenAI to integrate ad placements within advanced technology environments among communication stocks.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $766.7 million, growing by roughly 9.1% over the previous twelve-month period. The company reported net income of approximately $180.8 million, leading to a net margin of close to 23.6%. While revenue growth is more moderate than its peer, the positive net margin indicates the company is successfully converting a portion of its sales into actual profit.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.7x, suggesting a conservative level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at approximately 1.0x, indicating that current assets, such as cash and accounts receivable, roughly equal current liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $165.6 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 32.5% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Magnite is significantly dependent on advertising spend within the connected TV market, which could be impacted if programmatic auction adoption slows. The company also deals with high customer concentration, as two buyers accounted for approximately 44% of its revenue in 2025. Furthermore, it faces intense competitive pressure from larger participants like The Trade Desk (TTD +2.48%) and PubMatic (PUBM +3.18%) while navigating a complex legal landscape involving litigation against major tech firms.

While AppLovin carries a higher price relative to its sales, both companies trade at very similar valuations when considering their future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with AppLovin. Advertisers are spending more on ads that deliver measurable results, and AppLovin's AI engine sits right in the middle of that, deciding which ad each person sees in mobile apps and, increasingly, online stores. And it's paying off in a big way. Revenue is up 55% year over year, and about two-thirds of every sales dollar ends up as profit.

The company isn't without baggage, though. It still leans heavily on mobile games, and it faces investor lawsuits and short-seller claims that it disputes. Still, I'm excited to see that its latest quarter beat the company's own targets by a wide margin.

Magnite is doing plenty right. It helps streaming services and publishers sell ad space, its streaming TV business is growing fast, and it earns a healthy profit. But it is a much smaller business growing more slowly, and a record midterm political-ad season gave last quarter a lift that is hard to repeat.

AppLovin, meanwhile, is growing much faster and has extraordinary profit margins, yet its stock isn't any pricier than Magnite's compared with the profits analysts expect. For long-term investors, an AI ad engine this profitable, at a similar price, makes AppLovin the better buy for 2027.

#3074. This Portable Spot Cleaner From Bissell Is an Affordable Alternative to the Shark StainForce on Black Friday

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

You don't need to buy a full-sized carpet cleaner for your pet's messes.

A carpet cleaner may not be your first thought for a Black Friday purchase, but it’s actually a great time to buy one, since one of my favorite new cleaners I’ve tested is on sale. The Bissell Little Green Mini Portable Carpet Cleaner is $85 at Amazon, down from its usual $130 price. That’s a $45 savings and, according to Amazon, its lowest price in 365 days. That’s considerably cheaper than the Shark StainForce, which goes for around $200 and is $130 for Black Friday.

The Bissell Little Green cleaner offers tons of cleaning power in a small package at a reasonable price, though there are one or two catches regarding portability and setup that are worth knowing about before you decide which one to buy.

The Bissell Little Green Mini is a powerful portable spot cleaner. / CNET/Ajay Kumar

The Bissell Little Green Mini is a corded portable spot cleaner, but it’s still lightweight at 7 pounds. Setup is definitely a little more involved, with a clean water tank that you need to mix cleaning solution into and the need to have an AC outlet somewhere in the area. The trade-off is a significantly deeper, more powerful cleaning than what you get with a handheld battery-powered spot cleaner like the Shark StainForce. Using the Little Green on the toughest and oldest dried stains left by my pukey old man cat left me impressed with just how deeply it cleaned my carpets. The pristine result makes this corded cleaner well worth the extra setup, and even at full price ($130), you won’t find fault with its power or portability.

At $85, its lowest price in a year on Amazon, the Bissell Little Green Mini is an easy buy if you have pets and carpet.

Shark StainForce cleaning a stain off my carpet. / Ajay Kumar/CNET

The Shark StainForce is a unique handheld vacuum because it doesn’t just clean dry messes — it’s primarily intended to remove stains and wet messes. It resembles other handheld vacuums, but comes with a caddy and a custom Shark stain cleaner that mixes a deep cleaner and oxy cleaner in the spray bottle to lift stains.

It works incredibly well — I was blown away by how easily it lifted the worst messes off my white carpets. It removed yellow cat puke stains, wine stains and tomato sauce off both the carpet and couch. It works equally well for older dried stains and wet stains, using a mix of the stain cleaner spray and agitation with the included rubber scrubbing brush head that suctions up the mess at the same time. There’s also a smaller nozzle-brush cleaner included for tight spots.

The StainForce will suction up dry waste like cat hair and chunks of half-digested cat food, but the waste tank is fairly small, and it’s not really meant for dry cleaning of a large area due to the limited battery life.

The tank will also need to be cleaned out and dried after every use because wet messes will fester and smell if left too long. With all that said, this is the only portable spot cleaner I’ve seen with the design and usability of a handheld vacuum, which makes it an excellent choice if your primary need is portable spot cleaning. The $200 price may sound steep, but I’ve never seen a compact cleaner as good at tackling such tough stains.

I love the Shark StainForce for its service as a grab-and-go cleaner. It’s cordless, it lives in its caddy ready to go, and for a fresh spill I can spray, scrub, and suction in under a minute with no setup at all. I’ve used it on my cats’ worst messes, including hairballs, vomit from eating too fast, and dirty paws tracked in from the litter box. It works remarkably well for something so small and it’s still the go-to cleaner for my wife and I. The dual-spray bottle that comes with it does an incredible job of lifting stains, even from my white carpet.

Here I am scrubbing away with the StainForce powered on. You can still see some stain, but it’s going away.

The Little Green Mini is a different kind of machine, and that difference shows in the results. On a day when my cats were in rare form and decided to throw up on the bedroom carpet three times in a row, I knew a small portable cleaner like the StainForce wouldn’t cut it, not with the sheer quantity of debris they’d left behind.

I pulled the Bissell Little Green, which, worth acknowledging, is corded. That means more setup: fill the 16-ounce clean tank with water and the included Oxy formula, plug in the 12-foot cord, and work within reach of the cord and its 4-foot hose. It’s still light at just 7 pounds, and it has a useful handle for moving it from room to room.

The StainForce, by contrast, has no clean tank at all. You spray from a separate bottle and only a tiny dirty-water collection tank of under 5 ounces, with about 15 minutes of battery before it needs a recharge. The Mini’s clean and dirty tanks (16 and 13.5 ounces) are much bigger, and because it’s plugged in, it never runs out of power mid-clean.

That proved to be the lifesaver in cleaning my cat’s horrible messes. The Bissell generously saturated the stain with its built-in sprayer that can dispense water and cleaning solution straight from the hose. The hose digs in deep, rinsing and pulling stains, mess and dirt from deep out of the carpet layers. The larger chunks were safely suctioned into the dirty tank, along with the used water.

What I can say is that it did an excellent job of deep-cleaning stains from the carpet — noticeably deeper than the StainForce. It completely removed our cat’s mess, with no trace left behind, though our carpets were left a little moist. My wife’s verdict was that she’s never seen the carpets so clean before and she audibly wondered if it was worth investing in a full-size carpet cleaner because clearly the StainForce and vacuuming aren’t cutting it.

If you want the fastest possible cleanup for a fresh spill, get the Shark StainForce; it’s hard to beat a cordless cleaner with zero setup. For a smaller mess that I just want to get off my carpet, the StainForce more than does its job. But if your problem is stains that have soaked into the carpet, the Bissell Little Green Mini is the better cleaner, and at $85 on Black Friday — its lowest Amazon price in a year — it’s $45 less than the StainForce right now. It’s the one I’d buy for a house with pets, kids and carpets where you don’t want a big and bulky carpet cleaner and don’t want to worry about running out of charge for a bigger mess.

#3073. Here's Why Vera Therapeutics Stock Surged Today (Hint: It's Not Great News For Vertex Shareholders)

Some bad news from the developer of a rival drug lifted Vera's stock today.

By Lee Samaha – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:07PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vera Therapeutics ›

Vera Therapeutics (VERA +16.14%) stock was up more than 16% at midday today, but the increase didn't stem from any direct news from the company. Instead, the news came from a much larger company, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, (VRTX -5.24%) aiming to get a rival drug to Vera's Trutakna (atacicept) approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Vera's Trutakna is indicated for the treatment of primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) in adults. It received approval in the summer, and as you might imagine, a small biotechnology company like Vera, competing with a giant like Vertex with a $135 billion market cap, will push hard to establish Trutakna sales before Vertex can get its rival IgAN treatment drug, povetacicept, approved.

Vertex's drug is a real threat, not least as it's taken once every four weeks as opposed to Trutakna's once-a-week dosing.

As such, the recent news that the FDA had issued an extension "to the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) target action date for the Biologics License Application (BLA) for povetacicept for the treatment of IgA nephropathy (IgAN) by up to three months" reads like a shot in the arm for Vera's attempts to build sales.

Not only does it give Vera up to three months to build sales and get patients and physicians used to the treatment, but the fact that the extension was issued at all casts some doubt on ultimate approval.

Vertex's press release noted that the extension was due to an FDA information request, to which it promptly replied, prompting the FDA to require more time to review Vertex's submission. The sell-off in Vertex's stock may well be an overreaction to what could turn out to be merely a delay in approval. Still, that won't worry Vera too much, as it now has a few extra months to build Trutakna's market presence.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. #3070. Best Amazon Device Black Friday Deals I’ve Found (2026): Kindles, Echo Speakers

My house has been powered by Alexa and Amazon devices to some degree for the past decade. There's always an Alexa somewhere in my house, ready for a quick command, and it's an ecosystem I find myself coming back to again and again—especially since Amazon always has something new coming out to catch my eye.

While not everything is on sale from Amazon's various ecosystems (sorry if you've got an eye on one of the newest Kindles; those have yet to be on sale), there are several great Amazon devices you can get for a better price than ever during Black Friday. Here are all the best deals I've found on Amazon devices.

Looking for more discounts? Don't miss our guide to the Absolute Best Black Friday Deals. Hunting for Kindles and e-reader deals specifically? I've got a story for that, too.

This is my new bedside companion. The Echo Time feels more like a second-generation Echo Spot than the actual Echo Spot that came out two years ago; I'm curious why they didn't just make this a third-gen Spot. The Echo Time brings back the larger screen of the original Echo Spot and has a fun range of customizable clock faces you can use. It has sleep sensing to wake you up in the half-hour window before your official alarm time. You'll have to place it perfectly for that feature to work, but I've liked it a lot more than I expected. It also has no camera, so you can put it in your bedroom without any worries. It's expensive for what it is, so now is a great time to pick one up for yourself.

If you want an Amazon speaker that's small with plenty of sound power, the Echo Dot Max takes the small form of the long-popular Echo Dot and adds better sound and a smart-home hub. It even acts as a Wi-Fi extender if you're an Eero user. The price is great, too, for all you'll get.

Looking for something small but more affordable? The fifth-generation Echo Dot has improved sound over the older Dot models (though this one's getting up there in years, too) and has one of the cheapest price tags you'll find for a good Alexa-powered speaker.

If you want an Amazon-powered speaker with the best sound, the Amazon Echo Studio is always the answer. The original Echo Studio was my pick for sound quality, and the second generation still is. It also has a built-in smart home hub with Omnisense technology, spatial audio, and Dolby Atmos, and it can double as an Eero Wi-Fi extender.

The best of Amazon's latest generation of smart displays is the Echo Show 11. The Echo Show 8 is usually my go-to, but I think the Show 11 is worth the extra money for its bigger screen and better sound. It also has a built-in smart home hub, but it won't double as an Eero extender like the Studio or Dot Max.

As an avid note-taker, I love the Kindle Scribe. It's my go-to device to bring on a plane in case I get the itch to write a list or brainstorm an idea, while also knowing I could switch over to read my latest library book all in one device. The newer Kindle Scribes have been hard for me to recommend with the high price tag, but right now the third-gen Scribe is actually cheaper than the older second-gen model. I also really like the homepage design on the newer Scribes.

If you're looking to upgrade your e-reader experience, try a color Kindle. The first-generation Kindle Colorsoft is on sale, letting you add color highlights and see your book covers in full color (though a little muted since it's an e-paper screen). It's been hard to recommend because of the price and the lack of other features besides the color screen, but this deal price is pretty great, since it's actually a little cheaper than the older model for once.

You can also get a better price on an even bigger color screen with the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. It's on sale for a massive discount during Black Friday—$180 off—and adds a color screen to all the features you'd already get on the newest Kindle Scribe. It's a great device, though it does have a shorter battery life due to the color screen (Amazon rates it for up to eight weeks of reading or two weeks of writing). It’s only $50 more than buying the older, no-color second-gen model I've long loved.

If you're looking for the classic best Kindle to buy for a lower price, it's the Kindle Paperwhite. The newer version isn't on sale, but the 12th-gen version from 2024 is still great at an unbeatable price. You could spend a little less by buying the 2024 basic Kindle on sale, but I think the larger screen, a warm-toned front light, and longer battery life are well worth the extra cost. You can also get the Signature version on sale, but I wouldn't splurge on the older Signature, as the newer Signature will be compatible with Amazon's newest Kindle accessories, like the page-turn case.

If you want to control more things with your Echo speaker, these compact smart plugs from Amazon let you turn various devices in your home into voice-controlled ones. The plugs are a little expensive normally, but $15 per plug is a solid deal, so you can pick up a few of these for things like lamps.

These smart bulbs aren't Amazon-branded, but they are compatible with Amazon's smart home ecosystem. I love Cync's bulbs best out of all the ones I've tested, and you can get a two-pack for less than $30 during Black Friday sales.

One of my all-time favorite smart devices is a smart lock. If you want one that looks good without costing an arm and a leg, the Aqara Smart Lock U50 is the one I recommend. You will need a hub to let it have Wi-Fi and work with Amazon's smart home ecosystem, though.

If you want a TV powered by Amazon, our latest favorite from Amazon's lineup is actually its art TV. The Ember Artline is our favorite TV in Amazon’s lineup. Samsung’s The Frame feels more premium, but our team found the Artline plenty capable for displaying artwork, and it costs much less. It's a great option to get an art TV on a budget, especially during Black Friday.

If you already have a TV you love but wish it was controlled by Amazon, grabbing a Fire TV Stick will fix that. Our favorite of Amazon's streaming sticks is the Fire TV Stick 4K Max. You can get picture-in-picture from your security cameras that are connected to your Amazon ecosystem, and while it's designed with Prime Video in mind, you can install other streaming apps on here, too. You'll also get 16 GB of storage and Wi-Fi 6E support, plus Alexa voice control.

If you want a mesh Wi-Fi system, there's a lot to choose from these days. Eero has been around for a while and has a handful of different models, but the best one we've tried is the Eero Pro 7. It's our favorite for a simple system, and it also supports Alexa if you're already an Alexa user. Plus, newer speakers from Amazon can double as Eero extenders.

#3068. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.

Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

A wild week, a pricier turkey, and a Buffett reminder.

By Amanda Kish, CFA, CFP® and Robert Brokamp, CFP, EA – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:08PM EST

Happy Thanksgiving week from Advisor Insights, brought to you by The Motley Fool! We're serving a lighter plate this time so you can get to the leftover turkey. The market, meanwhile, spent the past week on a roller coaster with the safety bar optional: the S&P 500 sank 8.6% last week, its 12th-worst week since 1952, and then jumped 4.7% on Monday when Nvidia's co-founder walked back into the CEO's office. Your clients' plans didn't change in either direction, and that is the message worth carrying into this week's calls.

Trying to dodge the market's worst days without missing its best ones is like leaving a movie during the slow part: the plot twist always lands right as you reach for your coat. Last week's 8.6% slide and Monday's 4.7% snap-back were a very short course in exactly that.

Client-ready line: "Last week was ugly, and Monday was a reminder that the best days tend to show up right next to the worst ones. Your plan was built for weeks like this, so let's stay with it and revisit only if your goals or timeline change."

Sources: AP, CME Group, Freddie Mac, Cleveland Fed and Yardeni Research. Figures through Monday, Nov. 23.

The average cost of a classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10 this year, up 6% from 2025 and the first increase since the record $64.05 in 2022, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation’s 41st annual survey.

Why it matters to advisors: Clients feel inflation at the dinner table long before it shows up in a spreadsheet. Let's make sure your income plan is built to keep up."

#3065. Etihad’s New Credit Cards Are Primarily for Status Chasers

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The new cards offer perks like faster paths to status and elevated earning rates when purchasing tickets with partners.

Etihad Guest, the loyalty program of Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, is expanding its U.S. presence by introducing two new credit cards. Most people won’t get much value from these cards, but they can make sense for Etihad frequent flyers who want elite status.

The two cards are the Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card ($99 annual fee) and the Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card ($499 annual fee). Issued by the First National Bank of Omaha, both offer faster pathways to earning and maintaining elite status and the ability to earn extra miles on Etihad purchases.

They also offer extra miles on international transactions (neither has foreign transaction fees) and purchases with Etihad’s partner airlines, which include U.S. carriers like American Airlines and JetBlue Airways.

Here’s what you need to know about the cards.

The Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card comes with a $99 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the card is offering the following welcome offer for new applicants: Earn up to 40,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 10,000 miles after the first purchase and an additional 30,000 miles after spending $3,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: You’ll also get Etihad Silver status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account. Unlike most airlines, that entry-level status is enough to get you into the business class lounge when traveling through Etihad’s hub at Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International Airport.

You can retain that status by spending $20,000 a year on the card, or $3,000 a year on Etihad purchases.

The Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card comes with a $499 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

5 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

The only differences in rewards between the premium and standard cards are increased earning rates for eligible airline purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the premium card offers a higher welcome offer compared to the standard card: Earn up to 60,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 20,000 miles after the first purchase and 40,000 miles after spending $7,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: The premium card offers a faster track to elite status: automatic Silver status upon card approval and Gold status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account.

To maintain Gold status, you’ll need to spend $40,000 a year on the card, or $8,000 on Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you’ll have Silver status.

Wi-Fi benefit: After your first Etihad purchase, you’ll get 3,000 Etihad Guest miles, enough to cover Wi-Fi costs on a long-haul Etihad flight. You’ll then get those miles again after each cardholder anniversary.

Travel benefits: The card offers a statement credit for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck and select travel protections. If you already have a premium travel card, you might already have access to these perks.

The card also includes a Priority Pass lounge access membership. However, an Etihad spokesperson told NerdWallet that it’s the entry-level membership tier, so you’ll need to pay for yourself and guests each time you visit a Priority Pass lounge. Most premium credit cards in the U.S. that offer Priority Pass allow complimentary visits for at least the cardholder.

The Etihad cards make the most sense for Etihad’s frequent flyers who are flying to or connecting through Abu Dhabi several times a year.

That’s because the standard card’s accelerated pathway to Etihad Guest’s Silver status tier can unlock the ability to choose business class lounge access in Abu Dhabi as a status perk.

With the premium card, you get a fast track to Gold. If you select lounge access as a Gold status perk, you can not only bring a guest on the same flight into the lounge, but also access Etihad’s worldwide lounge network. That includes Etihad’s own lounges in New York and Washington, D.C., as well as most partner lounges at other Etihad destinations.

Bear in mind that while Etihad has many partnerships with other airlines, it’s not part of an alliance, so you don’t get lounge benefits when traveling on partners. You’ll need to be flying on an Etihad-operated flight to get into the lounge.

If you primarily fly with other carriers, then Etihad status will have limited upside for you.

However, the Priority Pass lounge membership that comes with the premium card does not have that restriction. You can access Priority Pass lounges while flying on any airline, although you’ll need to pay an additional per-person $35 fee each visit.

The earning rates on the Etihad cards are lackluster for everyday spenders. The bonus categories are for airline purchases with Etihad and its partners, as well as international spending.

That means your day-to-day purchases at home, like groceries, dining out and gas, earn only 1 mile per $1 spent.

Plus, there are more ways to earn Etihad Guest miles than spending on an Etihad credit card. For example, you can transfer points to Etihad Guest from Bilt Rewards, Capital One and Citi ThankYou.

Those programs offer cards that typically have better benefits and bonus categories, and they offer flexibility on how you can use your points and miles. With an Etihad card, you can only earn Etihad Guest miles, which expire after 18 months without qualifying flight activity. (If you’re not traveling on Etihad or its partners at least once every 18 months, then you definitely should not get the cards.)

One of the most interesting perks of the new cards is the bonus category for spending with Etihad partner airlines — 2 miles per $1 for the standard card and 3 miles per $1 for the premium version. Typically, airline credit cards reward customers only for spending on the airline, not partners.

There are better cards available, though. Some offer as many or even more points per $1 on flights purchased directly from airlines.

If you want the card solely to earn more Etihad Guest miles, then the answer for most people is no.

While you can earn more miles for purchases with Etihad and partner airlines, the earning rates aren’t attractive enough to justify the annual fees, especially when compared with existing cards with currencies that transfer to Etihad Guest.

Status chasers could benefit from the fast track to elite status — but you would need to be a fairly frequent Etihad flyer to really take advantage of your elite benefits.

You want a travel credit card that prioritizes what’s important to you. Here are some of the best travel credit cards of 2026:

Flexibility, point transfers and a large bonus: Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card

No annual fee: Wells Fargo Autograph® Card

Flat-rate travel rewards: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

Bonus travel rewards and high-end perks: Chase Sapphire Reserve®

Luxury perks: American Express Platinum Card®

Business travelers: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card

#3064. VSE: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its proprietary repair IP, not just distribution volume, is what gives VSE pricing power over the long term.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:09PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, VSE (VSEC +3.08%) announced record quarterly revenue of $541 million and raised its full-year outlook. For long-term investors, the company is converting aviation aftermarket demand into expanding profit margins and stronger cash generation. Three takeaways from management's comments highlight the key drivers.

VSE expanded its profit margins by combining a greater mix of higher-margin product and repair activity with cost synergies from recent acquisitions. Expanding adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) margins gives the company more cash to reinvest into its maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) network.

Management acquired Atech Turbine Components to add OEM-approved (original equipment manufacturer) repairs covering more than 300 part numbers to its portfolio. Owning proprietary intellectual property (IP) gives the business greater pricing power and insulates margins compared to standard component distribution.

Generating $47 million in quarterly free cash flow--cash left over after operating expenses and capital investments--helped VSE lower its adjusted net leverage ratio to 2.3 times debt to EBITDA. Stronger cash flow gives management flexibility to pay down debt from past acquisitions while continuing to fund organic repair expansion.

High fleet utilization and constrained new aircraft deliveries support steady repair volume, while exclusive distribution agreements protect pricing discipline. Operations teams are watching supply chain lead times to maintain shop throughput.

Combining proprietary repair IP with disciplined debt reduction positions the company to expand margins across commercial and general aviation.

Akai is continuing to open up its various music-making platforms with the MPC Sample 1.4 firmware. My favorite (and the most affordable) of the MPC samplers has become a popular home for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods. The company has decided, rather than fight it, to embrace the modding community. The latest update adds several new developer features, including support for the new SDK and custom Knob Effects plugins.

Plugins added to the appropriate folder on your microSD card are now automatically recognized and will appear at the bottom of the list in the Knob Effects menu. There’s also a Developer Mode, which lets you run scripts from the microSD card or access the sampler’s internal filesystem over USB, which will be handy for all those modders vibe-coding their own add-ons for the MPC. There’s also remote screen access for mirroring the display on an external monitor through the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app.

There are a few other nice updates, including flatten pad, which speeds up the resampling process for baking in effects on individual pads, and sequence record autoplay, which adds a looper-like experience. Akai also added a scale option to the 16-levels pad mode, so you’re not limited to 16 chromatic notes, and can instead play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major, or whatever key your track happens to be in.

For a look at some of the custom firmwares, effects, and other mods already available for the MPC Sample, check out this video from Loopop.

#3061. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

#3060. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#3059. Where Will AbbVie Stock Be in 5 Years? Its 2 Immunology Blockbusters Are Still Growing 20%-Plus per Year

Combined annual sales of Skyrizi and Rinvoq have surpassed Humira’s peak, and AbbVie’s pipeline is just getting started.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:17PM EST

Over the past five years, AbbVie (ABBV -0.88%) has more than tripled the S&P 500's total return, despite losing patent exclusivity for its biggest growth driver, Humira, an immunology medicine. The company's ability to overcome the loss of Humira, the best-selling drug in the industry's history, speaks volumes about its underlying business. But where might AbbVie be headed over the next five years? Let's see whether the drugmaker can continue beating the market.

AbbVie's core growth drivers in recent years have been Skyrizi and Rinvoq, two immunology drugs that have earned numerous indications overlapping with those of Humira. In fact, these two drugs have demonstrated superior efficacy compared to Humira across several indications. For instance, in a Phase 3 study in certain patients with plaque psoriasis, AbbVie pitted Skyrizi against Humira, and the former performed better.

Rinvoq also beat Humira in studies in some patients with rheumatoid arthritis. It's no wonder, then, that these two medicines already combine to generate more than Humira's $21.2 billion peak annual sales. Through Sept. 30, Skyrizi's revenue was $15.8 billion, up 25.6% year over year. Rinvoq's sales came in at $7.4 billion, 23.9% higher than the year-ago period. What's more, both have secured several expansions this year and should win more over the next five years.

And neither will lose patent exclusivity until at least 2033. Note that they have made it a habit to exceed expectations. AbbVie expects them to combine for more than $31 billion in sales this year. It had initially set a $31 billion combined target for 2027 (and even that 2027 guidance was $4 billion above a previous one).

True, the competitive landscape will evolve over the next few years. That could be a problem for AbbVie. But even with that caveat, we can expect Skyrizi and Rinvoq to continue performing well over the medium term.

Five years is enough time for AbbVie to launch several new products that will help it improve its financial results and overcome challenges, including government-led drug price negotiations in the U.S., which could reduce sales for some of its products. The pharmaceutical leader boasts several promising candidates investors should keep an eye on. One of the most promising is zumilokibart, an investigational medicine for eczema. Here's why this candidate looks particularly attractive.

According to some estimates, the eczema drug market was valued at $21 billion last year and could rise to $46 billion by 2034. It's a highly competitive industry, but zumilokibart has shown promising efficacy data while also benefiting from a very convenient twice-a-year maintenance dosing schedule, something no currently approved medicine in the U.S. offers.

If zumilokibart performs well in Phase 3 studies and earns approval within the next five years, it could help strengthen AbbVie's portfolio and extend its lead in immunology. Another important candidate AbbVie is working on is ABBV-295, an investigational weight-loss medicine, perhaps one of the fastest-growing therapeutic areas in the industry.

AbbVie licensed ABBV-295 from a Denmark-based company. The weight loss drug market might be worth $150 billion by 2035, up from $15 billion in 2024. AbbVie's ABBV-295 is being investigated as a long-acting treatment and, if approved, may be administered once per month. Investors should also keep track of ABBV-295's progress over the next few years, and these two candidates are only the tip of the iceberg. AbbVie is developing many more brand-new drugs and could have an even stronger portfolio by 2031.

In the meantime, the company expects no major loss of patent exclusivity through the end of the decade.

The market is well aware of AbbVie's excellent prospects. That's why the drugmaker's shares have crushed broader equities this year. But is the stock too expensive? Not in my view. AbbVie is currently trading at 18.5x forward earnings, versus an average of 19.2x for healthcare stocks. One might argue that AbbVie is worth a premium over its peers, especially those in the pharmaceutical industry. Many drugmakers will face major patent cliffs by 2030, and few post sales and earnings growth as consistently as AbbVie's.

Further, AbbVie has an outstanding dividend program, having increased its payouts for 55 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King (a company with 50 or more consecutive dividend increases). Given all that, I'd value AbbVie slightly above 20x forward earnings. So, at current levels, the stock looks like a steal.

#3057. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

#3056. Should You Invest in Anthropic Stock Now or Wait? Here's What History Says.

The hype was fast, and the pullback was faster. Here's what past big tech IPOs suggest about buying now versus waiting.

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:19PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

If you wanted to purchase Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) stock last week but couldn't get shares at the initial public offering (IPO) price of $83, you didn't have to wait very long for another opportunity.

Anthropic stock closed at $97.17 on its first day of trading on the Nasdaq but fell below $83 by Nov. 24 -- just its fourth day as a publicly traded company.

I think that Anthropic is a great company, and I'm fired up about the IPO. But I also have no interest in investing anytime soon -- because I've seen way too many big tech stocks fall before they can find their footing.

History says some of the best opportunities to invest in technology companies have come several months after their much-anticipated IPOs.

According to Equity Comp Academy, citing research from Nasdaq (NDAQ +1.93%), more than 70% of technology stocks underperform after going public. And some of the biggest tech IPOs of 2026 have been particularly disappointing for investors who bought shares on the first day of trading.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS +5.08%) went public in May at $185 per share and closed its first day of trading at $311. Anyone who bought Cerebras stock at that price was sitting on a nearly 65% loss by the end of October, when shares traded at roughly $110.

And Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.83%) stock went from an IPO price of $135 in June to nearly $161 at the end of its first day of trading. But SpaceX shares are now about $127.

You can find similar examples going back several years. What's particularly interesting is how little time investors often had to wait to get those stocks at a discount to their IPO prices.

Data source: Author research, public Nasdaq data.

I also wouldn't get too hung up on the IPO price when deciding when to buy a stock. Investors who bought Cerebras stock at $185 after watching it soar to $311 may have thought they were getting a bargain. But they still could have saved themselves a lot of money by waiting.

Perhaps my favorite example is Meta Platforms (META +3.13%), which went public as Facebook in 2012 at $38 per share. The stock fell below its IPO price on its second day of trading and didn't get back to that level for 14 months.

Meta has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. Investors certainly didn't need to buy Facebook stock in May 2012 to become wealthy from owning it.

Established technology companies have years of quarterly earnings reports for investors to review, assessing how well management has met its projections and how Wall Street has valued the stock relative to its earnings or revenue.

But that's not the case with Anthropic -- or any big tech IPO. So it's no surprise that those companies see significant volatility in the first few days. Before I invest in Anthropic, I want more detail about how much it spends on computing infrastructure. Anthropic can have outstanding revenue growth and still be years away from generating the kind of profits that justify its valuation.

Am I risking paying more for Anthropic stock six months from now? Sure. Arm Holdings (ARM +6.22%) and Airbnb (ABNB +4.07%) both more than doubled in value in their first year as publicly traded companies, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

But I'd rather pay a little more for Anthropic stock after seeing a couple of quarterly earnings reports if those numbers give me greater conviction in the company's ability to make money.

Plenty of people have made fortunes investing in technology stocks without ever participating in an IPO. In the long run, buying based on business fundamentals rather than debut-day hype is the far more reliable path to wealth -- and I don't see why investing in Anthropic should be any different.
