#3055. 'Big Short' Investor Michael Burry Thinks This Chinese Stock Is Worth About 60% More Than Its Price. Should You Buy?

Burry has stopped betting against the Nasdaq and is putting his money into cheap stocks overseas, led by one Chinese e-commerce giant.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:33PM EST

Michael Burry made his name betting against U.S. housing before 2008, but lately, he's been betting on something far less popular: Chinese stocks.

In his Substack newsletter, Cassandra Unchained, Burry said he has closed out his remaining bearish bets on the Nasdaq-100 and now holds roughly a quarter of his portfolio in cash. What's left is tilted abroad. Among his largest positions are MercadoLibre (MELI +4.47%), Australian online retailer Temple & Webster and JD.com (JD +3.68%). Separately, stakes in Hong Kong-listed Tencent (TCEHY +3.85%), BYD (BYDDY -1.05%) and Meituan make up a little over a fifth of the portfolio.

Burry explained the overseas tilt simply by saying that U.S. stocks, in his view, are still expensive.

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

JD.com is one of China's largest online retailers, known for owning its own warehouses and delivery network. Burry puts its intrinsic value at roughly $45 a share, and with the stock at $27.35 on Friday, that implies upside of more than 60%. JD also trades at about 0.17 times sales, its lowest level on record. Burry's exposure includes call options that expire in 2029.

His timing has looked good so far. Chinese stocks posted their biggest gain in two years on Friday after Beijing signaled more support for its markets, and JD rose about 4%. The shares remain well below their 52-week high of $34.30.

Burry isn't done with semiconductor stocks, either. He sold most of his bearish put options on Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) as the stock fell this month, while saying his original thesis "still has legs." His plan, he wrote, is to bet against Nvidia again "nearer $200/share during a period of market optimism. That time is not now." Nvidia closed Friday at $150.49.

Chinese stocks also carry risks U.S. stocks don't, including shifting government policy, U.S.-China trade fights, and accounting rules that give investors less visibility. JD's low valuation partly reflects those risks, along with fierce price competition in Chinese e-commerce.

Meanwhile, Burry can change course in days, and he often does, but the core idea is worth borrowing. When a profitable market leader trades at a record-low valuation because of fear rather than collapsing fundamentals, patient investors can be paid for waiting. If you want exposure to e-commerce stocks in China, JD is a reasonable place to start, as a small position you're prepared to hold for years. Investors who'd rather avoid China-specific risk can apply the same lesson at home: build a watch list of quality tech stocks that have been knocked down, and buy in stages.

#3054. Why Did Redwire Stock Pop on Friday

After a 74% drop, Redwire stock could be a buy.

By Rich Smith – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:49PM EST

On a holiday-shortened Friday in a holiday-shortened week, space company Redwire (RDW +9.17%) stock was one of the market's strongest performers, rising nearly 10% at one point before closing the day up 7.6%.

And here's the strangest part: There doesn't appear to be any news to explain it. No analyst upgrades, no price target changes -- not so much as a press release from Redwire itself to explain the move.

So what got investors so excited about Redwire on Friday? My best guess is that they're looking ahead to next week, when Redwire will present Thursday and Friday in Wiesbaden, Germany, at the LANDEURO 2026 international defense symposium and exposition.

Redwire is scheduled to showcase "robust multi-domain capabilities," including its propane-powered fuel cells, Octopus sensors, and Stalker and Penguin UAVs, at the exhibition, and could potentially announce sales concluded at its end.

That's just a guess, however, and the mere potential for contract announcements seems a pretty thin reed to support a 7.6% increase in Redwire's stock price. That said, a lot of risk has been squeezed out of this stock in 2026.

Since peaking in late May, shares of the space and defense stock have shed 74% of their value to just $6 and change. That's well below the $10 per share Redwire cost at the time of its 2021 SPAC IPO.

Although free cash flow-negative and unprofitable (analysts polled by S&P Global Market Intelligence don't expect to see GAAP profits before 2029), Redwire trades below what I consider a fair valuation for unprofitable space stocks at just 3.1x trailing sales.

While not a sure thing, investors betting on Redwire Friday are correct: At this price, Redwire could bounce higher on just about any positive catalyst.

#3053. Mortgage Rates Today, Tuesday, November 24: Lower, But …

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates are down this morning, but could seesaw back up tomorrow.

Another day, another substantial swing. This one's lower, but don't count on it starting a trend: We keep seeing mortgage rates move back and forth, but no one's expecting rates to take a dive. If you're watching this space because you're waiting to refinance, it's unlikely your wait is about to end.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.)

My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

Strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Markets are currently anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#3052. BigBear.ai vs. Cerebras Systems: Which Artificial Intelligence Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Federal defense AI software or wafer-scale AI hardware: which stock belongs in your portfolio as 2027 approaches?

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 1:51PM EST

10 stocks we like better than BigBear.ai ›

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has created a divide between software providers and hardware infrastructure giants. Choosing between BigBear.ai (BBAI +6.92%) and Cerebras Systems (CBRS +5.08%) requires weighing government contracts against massive computing power.

BigBear.ai focuses on decision AI for defense and intelligence agencies, while Cerebras Systems builds massive wafer-scale processors to accelerate artificial intelligence model training. These companies represent two distinct paths into the growing AI market, offering investors a choice between specialized software and high-performance hardware.

BigBear.ai focuses on AI-powered decision intelligence software, positioning itself as a unique player among tech stocks serving the defense industry. It uses a land and expand strategy by deploying minimally viable products to evaluate the potential for long-term government contracts. Because it derives significant revenue from a limited number of defense and intelligence agencies, customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $142.1 million, reflecting a decrease of roughly 1.5% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of $180.2 million during this period. This performance highlights the challenges of scaling software services within the rigid budgetary cycles of government clients.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was zero, indicating a very low level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with assets that can be converted to cash within a year, was 1.8x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $46.3 million.

Cerebras Systems builds massive semiconductor infrastructure, including wafer-scale systems designed to train large-scale AI models more efficiently than traditional chips. Its systems are used by organizations in medical research, cryptography, and energy, while its infrastructure is deployed in data centers worldwide. This specialized focus helps the company target niche markets that require high-density computing power.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $755.8 million, which represents growth of 79.9% over the previous twelve-month period. Despite this rapid top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of $651.4 million. The significant growth illustrates the high demand for specialized AI hardware as developers race to build more complex models.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company had a debt-to-equity ratio of -0.5x, which indicates that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio was 2.1x, suggesting a solid ability to meet short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $392.8 million.

BigBear.ai faces substantial revenue concentration since a few government customers provide most of its funding, making it vulnerable to budget shifts or contract terminations. The company has also navigated operational hurdles, including a $76.7 million goodwill impairment in late 2026 and legal challenges related to historical accounting restatements. Furthermore, it depends on third-party cloud infrastructure from providers like Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%) and Amazon (AMZN +3.96%), to deliver its software.

Cerebras operates in a highly capital-intensive industry where it must compete against established giants and rapidly evolving technology standards. The company is currently reporting significant net losses and negative cash flow as it invests heavily in its unique wafer-scale technology. Because it seeks to disrupt a market dominated by massive competitors, any delays in manufacturing or shifts in AI architecture could threaten its market share.

BigBear.ai appears to be the more conservatively priced option because it carries a much lower P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Between BigBear.ai or Cerebras Systems for exposure to the artificial intelligence market, I would pick Cerebras. The company's proprietary semiconductor chip technology enables AI systems to operate at faster speeds than those offered by larger competitors. This contributed to Cerebras gaining AI tech giants OpenAI, Microsoft, and Oracle as customers.

Meanwhile, BigBear.ai saw sales sink in 2025 after the U.S. government performed budget cuts. The company's revenue is rebounding in 2026, with full-year sales forecasted to come in between $150 million to $165 million, up from 2025's $127.7 million. However, the fact that the federal government could cut funding to BigBear.ai last year suggests its technology is not critical.

Moreover, the software company's reliance on federal contracts keeps it exposed to sudden shifts to its top-line growth. Its stock's lower valuation reflects this vulnerability, and until BigBear.ai can expand outside government dependence, Cerebras' innovative chips provide a better path to a return on your investment despite its stock's higher valuation.

#3051. Black Friday Stock Deals: 7 Bargains Our Analysts Are Watching Now

A lower price tag doesn’t make a stock a bargain by default. As Warren Buffett’s quote reminds us, the key word is “quality” — some stocks are marked down for a reason.

By The Premium Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:55PM EST

10 stocks we like better than GE Vernova ›

It's Black Friday, and millions of shoppers will hit stores and websites for the biggest retail day of the year. Meanwhile, Wall Street is quietly running a clearance sale of its own.

Warren Buffett famously loves a good sale. "Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down," he once wrote.

The recent market sell-off has left plenty of high-quality businesses sitting on the clearance rack. We asked our analysts to name one stock they think is on sale right now, and why. Here's what they picked (as a reminder, these are personal views and not official Motley Fool recommendations, so be sure to do your own research before buying).

GE Vernova's (GEV +2.84%) business has rarely looked stronger, but its stock tells a different story. Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers require massive amounts of power, and the high-voltage transformers and gas turbines needed to deliver it are in short supply.

That demand pushed GE Vernova's backlog to $197 billion in the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, providing multi-year revenue visibility. Until a few months ago, the company didn't expect backlog to hit $200 billion before 2028. Its turbine factory slots are getting sold out through 2032, and it has struck a deal to acquire Trench Group for $9 billion, vertically integrating to secure critical grid parts.

GE Vernova ended Q3 with nearly $17 billion in cash, generated $5.4 billion in free cash flow, and doubled its stock buyback plan to $20 billion.

With the stock down nearly 32% over the past six months, I'd say this is one AI stock on sale you can't go wrong with.

Alphabet (GOOG +0.54%) (GOOGL +0.68%) stock has reached bargain-basement levels, trading around 21x forward earnings estimates, as investors worry about the company's hefty investment in the AI infrastructure build-out.

That said, Alphabet's spending helps serve existing demand, and the cloud backlog of $561 billion suggests a huge wave of revenue growth lies ahead. On top of this, Google Search's longtime search market dominance should support ongoing ad revenue growth. Still, Alphabet's main risk is lasting pressure on free cash flow if the AI spending deepens and drags on.

Despite enduring a rocky ride, Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) investors continue to prosper, with the stock outpacing the broader S&P 500 so far this year. It's easy to see why.

E-commerce sales climbed nearly 12% year over year this far in 2026, while its industry-leading cloud revenue from Amazon Web Services (AWS) jumped 35% -- thanks to strong enterprise adoption of the company's artificial intelligence services. The company has become the world's third-largest digital advertiser, with ad sales up 20%.

Wall Street expects Amazon to grow its top line by nearly 16% annually over the next five years. Yet for all that growth, Amazon is remarkably cheap, selling for just 21 times earnings, well below its average three-year multiple of 39. That's a price worthy of Black Friday.

As of Nov. 19, Nu Holdings (NU +4.45%) is down 29% in 2026. Most of that drop came from one painful Brazilian election week. But political noise tends to be temporary, and this too shall pass.

I bought my first shares on Oct. 26, right after the stock fell 17% in a day on progressive-leaning election results.

Meanwhile, the stock trades at 11 times forward earnings while the business grew sales 37% last quarter. That's a wide-open buying window, and I climbed through it with an open wallet.

Nu makes over $1 billion a quarter in bottom-line profit with a return on equity above 31%. It signed up 3.7 million new customers in Q3 alone. The company also just secured a banking license in Brazil with no extra capital strings attached. And there's the U.S. launch, with Visa alum Rob Livingston as the California-based CFO. Nu is no longer a one-country story (or even stricly a Latin American business), and innovation outlasts election cycles.

Lula gets another four years, and Brazilian borrowers are paying late more often. Brazilian politics and late-stage credit quality could keep Nu's stock bumpy for a while.

Quarterly revenue at Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) has grown twelvefold in a year to $17 billion. Wow. More remarkably, existing customers are spending 9X what they did a year earlier. Claude is evolving from a software subscription into a fundamental business resource. And Anthropic is approaching operating breakeven. Most of its reported net loss stems from non-cash accounting charges. With shares below their IPO price, investors are buying extraordinary enterprise customer demand at a discount to the long-term opportunity. This is a B2B juggernaut.

KLA (KLAC +4.96%) dominates the market for finding microscopic defects in semiconductor manufacturing. The more complex chips become, the more financially damaging each defect becomes. That makes KLA increasingly indispensable. Quarterly revenue rose 29%, while free cash flow reached $1.34 billion. Its growing population of installed machines also generates recurring service revenue. KLA benefits not merely from greater chip production but from the rising difficulty of making each chip. And 20-year CEO Richard Wallace, an unsung hero, is one of the best-performing leaders in technology.

BillionToOne (BLLN +2.38%) uses proprietary genetic technology to detect incredibly small amounts of DNA associated with pregnancy and cancer. Quarterly testing volume increased 25%, average selling prices rose 18%, and cancer revenue nearly doubled. Gross margins reached 71%, alongside positive operating profits and free cash flow. The December launch of a blood-only test for detecting residual cancer expands BLLN's opportunity. Unlike many young diagnostics companies, BillionToOne has demonstrated that scientific innovation can finance further scientific innovation. I expect this company to deliver top-line growth and rising returns on capital for a long time to come!I believe all three of these stocks will beat the market over the next five years and yet I also believe all three will be more volatile than the market.

A lower price tag doesn't make a stock a bargain by default. As Buffett's quote reminds us, the key word is "quality" -- some stocks are marked down for a reason.

So before you buy, ask two questions: Why did the price drop, and would you still want to own this business at full price? If the answer is yes, the discount is just a bonus. If the answer is yes, the discount is a bonus.

Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

#3042. RTX Unit Pratt & Whitney Wins $2.5 Billion Navy Contract

The company's aircraft engine subsidiary will perform work on the F-35 Lightning II fighter.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:01PM EST

Storied defense company RTX (RTX +1.17%) notched a win just before Thanksgiving with a new and sizable contract from the U.S. Navy. This is hardly the first contract it's secured with our nation's military, and it surely won't be the last.

Regardless, it's another feather in its cap and, hopefully, a sign of good things to come for both the company and Pratt & Whitney, its aircraft engine subsidiary. Here's some detail about the deal, and how it'll affect RTX.

On Wednesday evening, after the stock market closed for the Thanksgiving holiday, the Department of Defense (DoD) announced the award of the contract. Specifically, this is a nearly $2.53 billion award to Pratt & Whitney to deliver equipment and services for the F135 jet engine that powers the advanced F-35 Lightning II combat aircraft.

Per the DoD's press release on the award, it's an "undefinitized contract action with cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost, and fixed-price-incentive-fee contract line items" for the plane.

Put in less bureaucratic language, the arrangement is for the RTX subsidiary to begin work on the project now, with the understanding that certain terms (such as final payment) are to be finalized later. This is a fairly standard type of defense company contract with the U.S. military, used when there is some urgency to a project, or simply a need to keep one running consistently and smoothly.

Many experts consider the F-35 Lightning II to be the most advanced multi-role fighter aircraft in our arsenal today. Given that, the Navy needs to ensure there are minimal gaps in the fleet's repairs and upkeep.

The DoD added that the bulk of this work will be performed in corporate facilities or on military bases in this country. 14% is expected to be performed abroad, specifically in Italy, the U.K., Norway, the Netherlands, Japan, and Australia. The project is expected to be completed in November 2027. Defense was to obligate over $436 million upon contract award.

This wasn't a particularly surprising development, which is likely why the investor reaction to the news was muted (RTX's stock was up only 0.5% in pre-market trading on Friday). Much of this is due to the long history both Pratt & Whitney and RTX's legacy Raytheon business have with the F-35 project, which stretches back to its beginnings in the 1990s.

Additionally, RTX is a sprawling defense conglomerate that pulled in nearly $89 billion in revenue last year. Of course, $2.5 billion-plus is more than just a drop in the bucket, but it's not going to suddenly transform the company in a meaningful way.

That said, the new F-35 contract is sizable. The DoD's announcement was part of a broader press release detailing six recently-awarded contracts by branches of the U.S. military. RTX/Pratt & Whitney's was the largest and more than double No. 2, a $1.13 billion award from the Navy to Northrop Grumman (NOC +1.02%) for work on strategic communications aircraft. Outside of the Northrop Grumman contract, the others are in the tens of millions of dollars.

The DoD is also significantly increasing its reliance on RTX, as the new contract's ceiling is around 58% higher than the preceding sustainment award RTX and its subsidiary received in late 2025. So, at the very least, I'd take this as a significant act of confidence and trust in the company and its veteran engine specialist to perform mission-critical work during a time of increased global conflict. That's enough to keep me bullish on RTX's future.

#3039. Sports Betting and the Way We Make Money

The podcast takes a hard look at America’s booming sports-betting industry, revisiting the math behind the wagers and offering betting listeners an alternative: investing.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:24PM EST

In this episode of Motley Fool Rule Breaker Investing, Motley Fool co-founder David Gardner explores the world of sports betting, discussing the money made, the influence wielded by celebrities, and the legacy left behind.

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 4, 2026.

David Gardner: What if I told you there's an enormously popular way to put your money at risk, where the odds are stacked against you, the middleman takes a cut, and the more you play, the more likely you are to lose? What if some of America's most admired athletes and entertainers were being paid to encourage you to play that game? Well, that's sports betting in America today. This week, I want to talk about the math, the money, and something I care about even more: how we choose to make our money. I'm a believer in freedom, I'm a believer in investing, and I'm a believer that what we do with our influence matters. Sports betting and a few questions for some famous friends only on this week's Rule Breaker Investing.

Welcome back to Rule Breaker Investing. This week, something a little different. I'm going to speak about sports betting. Now, I've spoken about this before. In fact, I devoted a page and a half of my book Rule Breaker Investing to this subject, and I'm going to share that passage with you shortly. But first, why am I returning to it? Well, because sports betting seems to be everywhere these days, and I love sports. I bet you do, too. I've loved sports all my life. Increasingly, when I sit down to watch a football game, a baseball game, or a basketball game these days, I'm reminded that there's another game going on alongside the one that's on the field. Who's favored? What's the spread? What's the over-under? Who's going to score the next touchdown? Of course, would you like to put a little money on that? I find myself wondering whether we've reached a point where the business of betting on sports is beginning to crowd out, for some of us, the simple pleasure of watching sports. Just how big has this become? Well, according to the American Gaming Association in 2025, Americans placed nearly $167 billion in legal commercial sports bets. Yeah, that's “billion” with a B. How much did the sportsbooks keep after paying out their winners? Nearly $17 billion. That's about $0.10 of every dollar wagered. Think about that. $17 billion flowing net from sports bettors to the companies taking their bets in a single year. That's just sports betting.

Across casinos, online gambling, and sportsbooks, the American commercial gambling industry generated almost $79 billion in revenue last year. There's a new kid on the block: prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket among others. According to Pew Research Center, those two platforms alone recorded $53 billion in worldwide trading volume in July of this year, one month. Now, that's measured differently from sports betting, so we can't simply add those numbers together, yet much of that trading is now focused on sports. My point is simple. This is an enormous business, and it's getting bigger. Those billions flowing to the gambling operators, they're coming from somewhere, from where? From whom? Well, from the customers, their customers, from you. If you're their customer, that's your money they're taking hand over fist. Now, I want to make something clear up front. I believe sports betting should be legal. I've always believed that adults should be free to make our own decisions with our own money. That includes decisions that I might think are foolish. I've enjoyed friendly wagers myself over the years. There's nothing inherently wrong with two friends putting $5 on a game or the loser buying dinner. Yeah, I think there's an enormous difference between that and the industrial-scale business of persuading millions of people to bet and bet again and bet again.

This week, I want to ask three questions. First, what does the math tell us? Second, what distinguishes sports betting from stock market investing? Third, a question that matters very much to me. I hope you, too, does it matter how we make our money? Let's start with a little math. I've often said that investing in the stock market is a little like sailing. Imagine you and me sitting together in a sailboat, the wind pushing us forward. Well, that would be the stock market’s compounding positive returns. That wind is at our backs. When you're a stock market investor, the broad stock market consistently rises over time, even with, of course, the storm, and there will always be storms. Sometimes the wind blows right in our faces. Sometimes our boat gets tossed around. Over decades, though, investors have benefited from owning pieces of productive enterprises, companies that create goods and services, generate profits, and grow. Now, sports betting has a fundamentally different mathematical structure. Here's a simple example. Suppose you and I bet on opposite sides of a football game. We each have a 50% chance of winning. If we're just betting against each other, one of us wins, one of us loses. Between us, no wealth has been created.

Now introduce a sportsbook. A common arrangement requires you to risk $110 to win $100. So if you win, you make $100; if you lose, you're out $110. OK, so suppose you make 100 such bets, each one a genuine 50-50 proposition. You win 50 and lose 50. Well, on your 50 winners, you're going to make $5,000, and on your 50 losers, you're going to lose $5,500. Congratulations, you've gotten half your predictions right, and you've lost $500. You're a loser. That's not even including the time and the attention that you devoted to making those bets in the first place, which, by the way, might be just as expensive or even more so. Now, the rare skilled bettor may find favorable odds, and the precise mathematics are going to vary from wager to wager. The point is that the sportsbook’s margin — that middleman is creating a headwind that the typical bettor has to overcome in order just to break even.

And this is where I want to pull a page from my book Rule Breaker Investing. Last September, my book Rule Breaker Investing was published. Part 1 is the six habits of the Rule Breaker Investor. Part 2 is the six traits that we look for in Rule Breaker stocks. Then in Part 3, I discussed the six principles of Rule Breaker portfolio management. One of them, Principle number five, is that you get to invest the whole race, by which I mean that unlike horse race bettors who have to place their bets before the race, we stock market investors can pay attention to our investments over time while we're holding them as part owners and make better decisions as we learn. Here's what I wrote about sports betting, and I quote, "The key to principle number five is simple. Use what's happening in the race to make every additional investment you make during the race smarter.

This is in contrast to a raging new area of speculation in this era, sports betting, to which I briefly want to speak. Sports betting, of course, is all or nothing, and the bet has to be put down before the game is played. Sports bettors have numerous disadvantages compared to stock market investors. They routinely have to take all-or-nothing propositions. They pay a middleman, the house, up to 10% commission and have to put down all their money before the race or the game starts. It's regrettable how easy and attractive sports betting is made to sound when it's such a losing play, day in and day out. I'm hoping this book reaches many and helps clarify for them why their money is so much better invested in the stock market. The market tends to rise over time, you and me in the sailboat, the wind at our backs. Sports betting, by its nature, is zero-sum, and your expected return is always negative. The handicaps are set very effectively, whether we’re talking about a 6.5-point favorite in basketball or seven-to-five odds at a horse track. One bettor will win, the other will lose, and the house will always take its cut. Over time, almost all consistent sports bettors lose money. What happens to those who consistently invest over time? The difference is immense.

Though sports betting is now widely legal in the U.S., that doesn't make it a smart bet. I've made friendly wagers with friends for decades, which can make watching games more fun and stressful. But I look askance at big-volume betting and especially its influence on the media coverage of sports I love. A booming gambling industry does not reflect my best vision for our future. Sports betting, as has been said of state lotteries, functions broadly as yet another tax on imbeciles. While some bettors may see it differently, the reality is that over time, most will lose their money." Well, there you have it, my words in print from my book Rule Breaker Investing published a year ago.

Two quick clarifications. First, sports betting today does include live betting where you can place wagers while a game is underway. That particular distinction I drew about betting before the game isn't universally true. Second, when I speak about the house taking up to 10%, that's a shorthand for a common betting convention, rather than a universal commission on every dollar wagered. Though earlier, when I presented the $167 billion of gambled money, do you remember how much money the house did make? Yeah, its take was just about $17 billion, just about exactly 10% of what was wagered; it's simple math. On a side note, I also want to say something about that last phrase, tax on imbeciles. That's strong language. I certainly don't think everyone who places a sports bet is an imbecile. The phrase is intended to make us think about a system in which the average participant faces a mathematical disadvantage and keeps betting over and over. I especially want to add what I consider the biggest distinction between owning stock and making a bet. Even though you often hear people saying, both are just gambling.

The stock market, sports, they are fundamentally different when you own stock, you literally own an asset, part ownership of a domestic or foreign business, you are an owner. You own a piece of an enterprise that may create value for years or, even better, decades. When you make a sports bet, you have a wager on a short-term outcome. You're not an owner of the teams or the underlying economic activity. You're a speculator. You're typically paying a price to an intermediary of the house to make your bet. Over time, the typical bettor, as I said earlier, is fighting math. Now, I suspect many of those who are fighting math don't fully understand the math that they're fighting. If you add up all the winnings and losses across all the customers and the money that flows to the house, well, it means that collectively, their customers come out behind. Earlier, I mentioned making 100 $100 bets. Let's say you win half of them, so you win $100, 50 times; you lose the other 50. It sounds like breaking even, right? Except you don't. As we pointed out, you've paid the house $500 for the so-called entertainment of breaking even. That's a 5% loss on your $10,000 wager.

Now imagine if you’d simply invested that $10,000 instead: a 50-stock portfolio, $200 in each position, or just simply $10,000 plunked into an index fund. Imagine what happens to that money. It grows over the years, in fits and starts through ups and downs, but with the possibility of compounding into something much bigger. That is the real opportunity cost of sports betting, and it is massive. It's not just the money you lost. It's the wealth you never give yourself the chance to build. The house doesn't win every bet. It doesn't need to.

Its business model is built to win over time. Let me put that larger distinction as simply as I can. In the stock market, your success doesn't require my failure. If you and I both buy shares of a wonderful business and that business grows and prospers for 20 years, we both win, and the employees can win. The customers can win. Society can benefit from what that business creates. That's one of the beautiful things about capitalism at its best. Sports betting, again, a very different enterprise. The bookmaker makes its money by operating a market in wagers, and its customers collectively bear the cost of that business, collectively bear the cost of that business. We've talked about the math, and I hope we've talked about the money, and I hope especially to people who are new to the stock market and don't realize that it goes up over time and don't realize the opportunity cost they're paying by playing a losing game, putting their money down repeatedly in an expected negative return context.

I hope this is opening a few eyes, and dear listener, if you already knew these things, I hope you'll share it if you know, especially a younger person who doesn't know these things. I hope this short podcast will make its impression, maybe one or two points to close. I mentioned at the top. I've said this in past Rule Breaker Investing podcasts. I'm going to emphasize it again right here. I have always believed that how we make our money matters, not just how much — how. I love investing in businesses that make the world better. I love entrepreneurs who solve problems. I love companies that create products that people didn't know they needed that improve our lives, that open up new possibilities. I've spent much of my adult life trying to find and support those enterprises and recommend them to a worldwide Motley Fool membership. I want to ask a simple question. When we look back at the money we've made over our lifetimes, shouldn't we care about what we helped bring into the world along the way? Which brings me to a few people I'd like to address directly. I'm going to mention a few famous people here, and I want to be clear about my purpose.

This is no indictment. I'm not accusing anybody of breaking the law. I'm not questioning anyone's right to earn a living or to make an endorsement. I'm simply going to be asking a question. Is this how you want to make your money? Kevin Hart, you're one of America's most successful comedians. You've entertained millions of people. You've built an extraordinary career, and you've appeared in advertising for DraftKings. Nick Jonas, you've made music that people love, and you've joined Kevin in DraftKings campaigns. Now, is that something you guys will be proud to share with your grandkids? Is that the legacy you want to be building? Jamie Foxx, you're an Academy Award-winning actor, a musician, a remarkably talented entertainer. You've been a prominent spokesperson for BetMGM. Jon Hamm, another wonderful actor. You're also among BetMGM's ambassadors. Now, I wonder, gentlemen, whether you've thought carefully about what you're encouraging your audiences, something for your biggest fans to do.

LeBron James, you've been one of the greatest basketball players of all time, a businessman, a philanthropist, inspiration to millions. You previously promoted DraftKings, and now you're partnering with Polymarket. LeBron, you’ve spent your life winning; do you want to encourage your fans to play a game where, collectively, your fans are expected to lose? Peyton Manning, Eli Manning, two Super Bowl champions, you've lent your family's reputation to Caesar's sportsbook. Eli, you've appeared in Polymarket’s advertising as well. You know something about leadership. What responsibility comes with lending your credibility to a business whose customers, on average, lose money? Wayne Gretzky, the great one. You've been an ambassador for BetMGM. You've spent a lifetime making hockey better, inspiring generations of young athletes. What do you hope those same generations take away from your association with sports betting? Derek Jeter, captain of the Yankees five five-time World Series champion. Your BetMGM partnership has even included a Jeter-themed casino game. Got to ask, Derek, is a casino game really something that you want your legacy attached to?

I guess I could keep naming names, but you can see them in television advertisements, print, online, apps on your phone. They're everywhere. I'm just finding myself asking this question. What are you lending your reputation to? Just broadening it to every famous person who's involved in this industry. What are you normalizing for your fans? When somebody sees your face on an advertisement, what are you hoping they'll do next? What if they do it again tomorrow and next week and next year? Now I recognize that DraftKings and other operators promote so-called responsible gambling. They've developed tools intended to help people limit their betting.

OK, glad they're doing it. Yet the larger question remains. Your fans admire you. Some have followed you for decades. Some are young adults, just beginning to manage their own money. Some are parents trying to build a better future for their children. Do you really want them to become more active sports bettors? Do you believe that's going to make them smarter, happier, and richer? I don't know what most of these arrangements pay. I don't know the personal circumstances or motivations of the people I've mentioned, and I recognize that they may see these businesses as legitimate entertainment freely chosen by adults. I respect their freedom to make that judgment.

Now, I’ll recognize someone who has made a different choice: Victor Wembanyama, the extraordinary young San Antonio Spurs star, has publicly expressed his preference for promoting healthy habits and things that make people’s lives better rather than gambling. Victor, I appreciate that you're thinking about the influence you have and what you want to do with it. I appreciate you asking the question, how do I want to make money in this world? All right, shorter podcast this week, I'm going to close to every endorser and influencer of this wealth-extracting popular big business, which most of all, is targeting young men at the start of their financial adult lives. I ask, of all the ways you could be making money, is this one of the best ways you can imagine? There are lots of ways to make money in this world. Some make the world better. Some make it worse. Many fall somewhere in between. The more successful we become, the more choices we have about where our next dollar might come from. Ultimately, what will matter most about that dollar: how much it was worth, or how we earned it? That's a question for Kevin Hart, for LeBron James, for Peyton Manning, and for Derek Jeter and every other famous celebrity or athlete involving themselves today in this industry. By the way, it's not just a question for them. It's a question for you and for me, too. How will we choose to make our money?

TL;DR: Rising inflation could, counterintuitively, help push mortgage rates further down.

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3033. Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before CEO Jensen Huang Testifies in Front of Congress on Dec. 1 and Dec. 3?

Huang is set to testify before Congress next week, both publicly and behind closed doors.

By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:28PM EST

Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks.

Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching.

On Dec. 1, Huang will testify before the U.S. House of Representatives' Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committee, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter will also testify before the same committees on Dec. 2. Both hearings will be private, with transcripts not expected to be published publicly for some time.

But on Dec. 3, Huang will testify at a live hearing before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, an event that will be closely monitored by all investors. Should investors buy Nvidia stock before these hearings?

While President Donald Trump has come out in support of Huang and claims to have played a role in his reinstatement, the hearings will help reveal how other lawmakers feel about Huang and what's going on with Nvidia.

"The market volatility and nervousness is centered on a number of issues that the Jensen soap opera has highlighted front and center," Yorkville Ives analyst and Managing Partner Dan Ives wrote in a recent research note, according to Business Insider. "Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC."

Huang's reinstatement as CEO led to a swift surge in the stock, but since then, shares have been pressured by lingering investor concerns about the company.

Multiple reports suggest that a woman Huang had an affair with, named Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at the Singaporean data center company MegaSpeed, may have facilitated a network that diverted advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

Investors are trying to understand how much prior demand for Nvidia's chips, if any, may have been driven by similar sources. Since the scandal came to light, the U.S. Commerce Department has moved to close loopholes and tighten export controls that may have allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely.

The Commerce Department is now also requiring companies in select countries, such as Singapore and Indonesia, to obtain a license before transferring or reexporting advanced chips from U.S. companies.

In his note, Ives said he believes the impact on revenue resulting from such export controls is "a containable 15% to 20% at most." Still, that's a significant amount, and while some of it is priced in, Nvidia stock could certainly face more pressure if it believed future demand wouldn't be as strong.

Given that Wall Street analysts like Ives are already contemplating what would happen to Nvidia's revenue if increased export restrictions lower demand, or some sources of demand abroad are closed off, it's clear the market is pricing in at least some of the potential impact.

Still, Wall Street consensus estimates expect Nvidia to earn $16.61 per share on an adjusted basis for its fiscal year 2028 ending in late January 2028. That means Nvidia trades at just 9x forward earnings, so the valuation is attractive.

But as we've seen through this whole debacle, things can change in a hurry, so I would never tell investors to buy a stock based on a near-term event like a Congressional hearing.

With Nvidia trading at a cheap level, I think investors can purchase a position to hold long term. But I do not believe that the majority of a traditional stock portfolio should be concentrated in Nvidia or AI stocks, as much uncertainty remains.

#3030. Churchill Downs: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

A new racing series and flexible gaming licenses position the company to monetize beyond its iconic annual event.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:28PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Churchill Downs ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, Churchill Downs (CHDN +1.57%) announced record net revenue of $696 million and adjusted EBITDA, a metric tracking cash operating profit, of $264 million. The company is divesting lower-margin regional casinos to refocus capital on its core horse racing and gaming venues. Three key takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

Management expects to execute sales transactions for nine regional casino properties by the end of 2026. Selling these non-core gaming properties narrows the portfolio around higher-return assets. The transaction proceeds will allow the business to cut debt, repurchase shares under a newly authorized $750 million program, and fund expansion at Churchill Downs Racetrack.

Starting in 2027, the company is launching a five-month racing series across three premier tracks to extend fan engagement past Derby Week. By connecting marquee events into a single season-long narrative, management creates new long-term revenue channels.

A new casino in Petersburg increased regional competition for central Virginia gaming venues. However, management retains statutory authority to shift historical racing machines (HRMs), which are video gaming terminals driven by past race results, and operational licenses across the state to maximize returns in underserved locations.

Ticket sales for the 153rd Kentucky Derby are pacing 25% ahead of last year's rate as customer demand expands. Long-term value relies on pricing power at Churchill Downs Racetrack, expanding historical racing machine floors, and growing the TwinSpires wagering platform.

Management is working to lower bank leverage below 3.0x following casino sales while compounding cash flow across core platforms.

Winter is the ideal time to make progress on your financial goals.

When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

“You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”

One important component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

“We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”

Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

“Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”

Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman says.

If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

Once you’ve outlined those big goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird says.

He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird says.

“Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”

Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

With credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.)

“High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman says. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

Even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

“It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”

“Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he says. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”

#3017. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

You don’t need a basement bunker, but keeping some cash on hand might help.

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:

Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?)

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”

If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge says. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”

Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” said Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”
