#3015. Nvidia, Micron, and Sandisk Trade at Half the S&P 500’s Forward P/E. They Are All Genius Buys.

The market has mispriced these tech stocks.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:38PM EST

Comparing stocks to an index like the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) is a great way to assess their relative valuation. For example, if a stock is trading at an earnings ratio that’s cheaper than the market average, there should be a good reason for that.

The same goes with being more expensive. What investors should often be looking for is stocks that are not valued marginally above or below the S&P 500, but under it by an amount significant enough to raise eyebrows when the business is assessed.

Three that are trading at massive discounts from the S&P 500 are Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), Sandisk (SNDK +15.96%), and Micron Technology (MU +7.60%). All three are posting monster growth figures, so if the reasons they trade at a discount don't hold water, then they are well worth buying at these prices.

First, let's look at the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500, which is currently 18. With Micron, Sandisk, and Nvidia's fiscal year not ending in the next 12 months exactly, there is a bit of a mismatch on end dates in this analysis. However, the offsetting periods aren’t so large that the difference really matters in this case.

Both Sandisk and Micron are in their fiscal year 2027s right now, and each trades at a substantial discount to the market.

At just 3.6 times forward earnings, Micron looks like a bargain. Sandisk is even cheaper at 2.7 times forward earnings. That means these two are anywhere from five to six times cheaper than the S&P 500 is right now. That's a deep discount, but why do these two trade that low?

Both companies make memory chips, which have two important use cases in AI: providing quick-access memory for computing units and long-term data storage. Demand for these chips from companies building data centers has exceeded the memory industry’s global production capacity. As a result, the memory market is now in a severely supply-constrained state.

Simple economics states that when demand is high and supply is low, prices rise. That is exactly what has happened, and Micron and Sandisk have seen their revenues and profits skyrocket over the past year.

The low prices of these two stocks reflect the market’s bet that these conditions won't last and that a downturn in the memory market is inevitable.  However, Micron's management team told investors during its most recent earnings call that it anticipates that memory market conditions will tighten even further in 2027 and 2028. So, these two companies have nothing to worry about in the short term, and that makes their stocks look like absolute bargains in the meantime.

The turmoil around GPU maker Nvidia has been hard to ignore if you're an investor. Furthermore, just because Jensen Huang is back in the CEO role doesn't mean that the company is in the clear. There are still concerns about whether some of Nvidia’s most powerful processors reached customers in China, despite U.S. trade rules that ban their export to that country.

We'll learn more about what's going on with Nvidia when Huang testifies before Congress, but ongoing investigations could still reveal problems that impact the business.

However, given that Huang was willing to return to the CEO role, I'd say the likelihood of anything too drastic happening is low; otherwise, he might have taken the opportunity to run for the hills.

As a result of its troubles, Nvidia trades at 9.4 times 1-year forward earnings, a low price.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That's about half the price of the S&P 500, but still more expensive than Sandisk or Micron. Regardless, I think all three are worthy buys at this price point, because they are all primed to benefit from the booming AI arms race.

#3010. Anthropic’s IPO Hangover and the Worst Acquisitions Ever

Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has barely begun trading, but investors are already questioning whether its trillion-dollar valuation can hold up.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:46PM EST

Editor's note: This podcast was recorded before Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia CEO.

In this podcast, Motley Fool contributors Travis Hoium and Lou Whiteman, and Motley Fool analyst Jason Moser discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

Travis Hoium: Anthropic IPO is here, and Motley Fool and Hidden Gems Investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing. I'm Travis Hoium, I'm joined today by Lou Whiteman and Jason Moser. Guys, we had the big event, the Super Bowl of the year Anthropic IPO happened this week. I think they hit a $2 trillion valuation for about two minutes. Then things started to fall apart. We're already in bear market territory, which means the stock is down 20% from its high. As we're recording early on Friday, Jason, the stock is down 11%, nearly back to its IPO price. When you stock high level, what do you think about an IPO like this? Is this a big deal? Is this just, you know, kind of par for the course?

Jason Moser: Not often we get $1 trillion company coming around. Well, I love the par for the course there, Travis, as they say, lifelong golfer, that it resonates with me. Thank you. I think it is par for the course. We see this, time and time again. I mean, this is a massive IPO with a company that is clearly going to play a very important role in our economy in the development the evolution of technology and whatnot. There's a lot of emotion that comes with an IPO like this. We see these kinds of movements all the time. I think I don't read too much into it. I think most of us were probably optimistic about Anthropic as a business. I am personally. I mean, I think, look at companies like Anthropic and SpaceX, and I think, Wow, directionally, these companies are correct. I mean, that's where the world is headed. It's just a matter of how they get there. I think for Anthropic, it's just going to be learning more, I think the biggest question for me is how Anthropic gets beyond being just, and I say just, but just being an enterprise business first and foremost. I mean, you've got basically like 80% of the revenue that they make comes from usage fees with subscriptions representing the rest of that. I wonder how it's going to bridge the gap from being an enterprise business to also being like a consumer-facing business, something that Google has done so well for so long. #3001. Pfizer's 6% Yield vs. AbbVie's 53-Year Dividend Streak: Which Stock Is the Better Buy?

Pfizer is facing down big patent expirations, but that's pretty normal in the drug sector.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:05PM EST

AbbVie's (ABBV -0.88%) 2.3% dividend yield pales in comparison to Pfizer's (PFE +0.21%) 6%. But it is important to recognize that the average drug company's yield is only 1.3% and the broader market's yield is just 1%, so AbbVie's yield isn't exactly small. Here's why conservative dividend investors wouldn't be making a mistake by buying AbbVie, but if you can handle a little uncertainty, Pfizer's much higher yield may end up being the better option.

One of the big positives of AbbVie as an investment is that it is a Dividend King. That means that the company has increased its dividend annually for 50+ consecutive years (53 to be specific), which is not something that happens by accident. It requires a strong business model that is executed well in both good and bad markets. The only problem here is that AbbVie hasn't actually existed for 50 years. It was created in 2013 when it was spun off from Abbott Laboratories (ABT +0.07%). It retained Abbott's dividend record and then, to AbbVie's credit, continued to raise its dividend each year.

Still, it probably isn't appropriate to give AbbVie full credit for its Dividend King status. You should pay extra attention to its actual business, which is well-run and fairly well-positioned. It has strong positions in immunology and oncology. Meanwhile, the drug maker's aesthetics business doesn't face the same patent risks as other drug niches because brand names are important differentiators. As a business, it is highly desirable.

There's just one small problem: the stock isn't cheap. Its price-to-sales ratio is 7.9x compared to a five-year average of 5.4x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 50x compared to a five-year average of 41x. You are paying full fair, if not more, for the stock's above-average yield.

That's where Pfizer starts to look relatively attractive. Not only is its dividend yield likely to be highly attractive to income seekers, but the stock is also much cheaper than AbbVie. Pfizer's 2.5x P/S ratio is in line with its five-year average and far lower than AbbVie's 7.9x. Pfizer's P/E ratio is 40x, which is biased higher by one-time charges and still lower than AbbVie's 50x. If you use the $3.00 per share midpoint of Pfizer's 2026 adjusted earnings guidance, the P/E is around 10x. That's below the stock's nearly 14x five-year average.

A big yield from a cheap stock will likely have more appeal than a smaller yield from an expensive stock for most investors. But there are issues to consider, most notably Pfizer's upcoming patent expirations in 2028 (Eliquis) and 2031 (Vyndamax). Those are big deals and will likely result in a substantial decline in revenues and earnings. The thing is, patent expirations are entirely normal in the pharmaceutical sector. Pfizer is working hard to develop new drugs to offset the hit, but sometimes the timing doesn't perfectly align.

Still, given the company's strong history, which dates back to the mid-1800s, it seems highly likely that it will manage this patent expiration cycle, just as it has many times before. As for the dividend, the company is publicly supportive of it and continues to tell investors that its long-term goal is to grow the payment. And even if there were a 50% dividend cut, which seems like a reasonable worst-case scenario, the yield would still be higher than AbbVie's 2.3%.

If you are a risk-averse investor who simply can't tolerate any kind of uncertainty, AbbVie is a perfectly fine, though perhaps expensive, stock to buy. However, Pfizer's higher yield and more attractive valuation will probably make it a better option, assuming you believe it can muddle through its patent-expiration issues, as it has many times before. Indeed, the risk-versus-reward balance is likely tilted toward reward for long-term dividend investors.

#2998. Constellation Energy: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Nuclear uprates add nearly 1,200 megawatts faster and cheaper than new plants, a capacity edge that matters as grid bottlenecks tighten.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:09PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Constellation Energy ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 9, 2026, Constellation Energy (CEG +1.20%) raised its full-year adjusted operating earnings guidance to $12.50 to $12.80 per share. The company is securing multi-decade power contracts that lock in predictable cash flow far into the 2040s. Three things management said stand out.

Management is shifting the business away from short-term commodity price swings toward long-term agreements. By securing 20-year power purchase commitments with major technology companies, Constellation locks in revenues well above the nuclear Production Tax Credit (PTC), a federal tax incentive for clean power generation.

Constellation Energy is expanding output through nuclear uprates, which are projects that increase power generation capacity at existing facilities. Adding nearly 1,200 megawatts through uprates allows the business to meet surging electricity demand more quickly and at lower cost than by constructing new power plants.

To address electricity grid bottlenecks, management launched Constellation Peak+, a commercial product structure that pairs nuclear generation with backup power or demand response, in which customers reduce power usage during peak-demand hours. This structure gives data centers a fast, regulatory-compliant pathway to secure reliable electricity in PJM Interconnection, the regional grid operator serving the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest.

Operational execution remains sharp across the generation fleet, driving a guidance raise after nuclear plants recorded a 99.2% capacity factor during peak summer demand. That commercial and operational strength reinforces a track record of consistent outperformance.

An unmatched nuclear asset footprint, investment-grade customer counterparties, and strong balance-sheet flexibility position the company to capture ongoing clean-energy demand. Strategic priorities center on capital allocation discipline, opportunistic share buybacks, and the expansion of long-term contract coverage across the fleet.

#2989. Is the AI Trade Ending?

Investors backing AI have a lot to think about.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:19PM EST

In this podcast, Motley Fool contributors Travis Hoium and Lou Whiteman and Motley Fool analyst Emily Flippen discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 6, 2026.

Travis Hoium: Is the AI trade ending? Motley Fool Hidden Gems investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool Hidden Gem’s investing. I'm Travis Hoium, joined today by Lou Whiteman and Emily Flippen. Guys, we've got to start with the big news for the week. We had some panic in the markets, I would say, on Thursday. The NASDAQ, I believe, was down about 5%. S&P 500 down four or 5%. Really big moves in some of the big names that have had a really great year in the AI trade. Lou, the broad question is, is this AI trade dead? Is it ending? Is it slowing down? Where does your head go after a week like this?

Lou Whiteman: I don't think it's dead by any means, and I actually don't think it's necessarily slowing down, but I think we are shifting, both and more in the perception of it on our side, but I think we are seeing a shift, and that will affect investments and the companies we're looking at. I think the land grab period might be over. For the last two years, it was a clear mandate: just go spend. The risk was under-investing. It was never over-investing. We all knew this was a lot of money, but we accepted that. The benefit of the doubt is gone. The market psychology is beginning to turn towards return of investment. I think it was happening already. I don't necessarily think it was just an election thing, but definitely, I think the election was the cherry on the top. I think, again, I think it can still work from here. I think these companies will continue to invest. But just this Pollyanna world where, don't worry, it will all work out in the end, which you can get a premium because you have certainty there. You assign a premium to that certainty. That certainty is gone, and people are asking questions, and that will affect valuation, and it might, long term, out.

Travis Hoium: Emily, the interesting thing this week was that we did have the election, which we don't, as investors want to focus too much on that, but it was such an interesting reaction because after-hours trading on Tuesday had the markets falling fairly significantly, a couple of percentage points. Then Wednesday was a phenomenal day. We knew the results of the election on Wednesday. Then Thursday was a terrible day. It seems like the market is just confused with itself what it wants to think about both the election. Then, like Lou said, I think maybe this is just bringing some reality and going, Wait a second. Nobody wants data centers in their backyard, and that was true across the board, no matter who won on Tuesday. It is such a strange back-and-forth that we've had just in the past three or four days.

Emily Flippen: My take might not age well, so you can hold me to it later. But I think the market was trying to do two things. One is price in the risk of new political pressure on things like data centers, which is likely going to be a big focus point when you look at our new congressional setup, but also pricing in the reality that is CapEx and spending for things like AI indicate continued growth. That's what's causing the volatility. You have two things that are acting against each other. I'm not trying to dismiss the pain that people experience this week, but I personally don't think we'll ever see a sustained downturn in AI spending or AI bubble, so to speak, until we start to see hyperscalers turning off their CapEx spend. So far, we don't have any indication that that is the case, and we likely won't get that indication until we get next quarter's earnings, when we start to get guidance for things like CapEx into fiscal year 2027.

Travis Hoium: I think you're right that right now we don't see a slowdown in CapEx spending, but I try to study history on these kinds of things. If you look at what happened in the.com buildout, which on the telecom side is probably the most analogous thing we have to this current AI buildout. There was growth in that CapEx through the end of 2000. At least the December quarter of 2000, but the market peaked in March of 2000. By a year later, the NASDAQ 100 was down about 50%. As the market is always forward-looking, are we running a risk where whether they want to blame it on political pressure and regulations or whether they want to say, Hey, you know what? Borrowing costs are going up, so we got to pull back. Stock prices are down. We don't have this mandate that Lou talked about to spend as much as we want in the future. If that spending starts to slow, typically the market drops before we actually hear that in earnings calls. Is that at least on your mind when you're looking, especially at these big cap companies, and then even down the value chain?

Emily Flippen: Well, I actually think that there are two separate things. one side, we have, say, the Telecom Giants, for instance, big hardware plays that are the recipients of CapEx spend from, let's say, the hyperscalers today.

Travis Hoium: Do you put Nvidia in that category, too?

Emily Flippen: I would put Nvidia in that category. That's a great example. People look towards Nvidia whenever they report earnings as the AI leader. But in practice, Nvidia is a lagging indicator of spend that has already happened. We can continue to see growth with Nvidia while the market is selling off because what they're selling off, to your point, is what the future expectations are. I personally think a lot of those future expectations and regards to growth and CapEx come from a lot of these large software players that can, to your point, turn off and turn on that dial very quickly, and then that will dovetail all the way down the chain to the big hardware players.

Travis Hoium: Lou, we got to talk a little bit about mindset on a week like this because I think this is where the Motley Fools' long-term mindset, having a multi-year, maybe even multi-decade view, really comes into play because we have no idea what's going to happen with the market tomorrow or the next or next week. But if you have a view on what's going to happen five years from now, ten years from now, that should put things in your favor a little bit. How are you handling a week like this? Is there any actions that you're taking? Are you doing nothing? Are you finding opportunities? Where are you at as an investor?

Lou Whiteman: I actually had the best place to be on Thursday when all this was going down. I was in a small metal tube without any access. I was on an airplane.

Travis Hoium: Were you testing Starling for us?

Lou Whiteman: No, I was on Delta. The Wi-Fi was fine, but I wasn't doing a lot of trading. But actually, it's perfect. I was handcuffed, even if I wanted to, but look, it's so easy to get caught up in the moment, and it is, like I said, I do think there's a shift here, and I don't want to whistle past it because I do think, to butcher the old fable, once nobody ever could picture the emperor with his clothes on again after they all realized. I think change can be permanent here, but I still think, if you look at it, AI is not going away. Whatever it's going to become, whether it's the imaginary friend on your shoulder or just a productivity machine, there is a real there there, and there are long-term trends that you can look at there. There was a lot of carnage just almost everywhere. There was risk on, including my beloved space sector. I think that I can still see. I don't know what the next six months are going to look like. I'm a little nervous about the next six months. Looking long term, there are trends that are going to work out, and I do think there will be buying opportunities. I do think, look, even going back to 1999, there were winners there. One of the lessons is that there's never been a bubble, and this is a bubble. It doesn't mean it's going to burst, but anytime there's enthusiasm about a sector, and it gets too crazy valuations, it's a bubble. May it long last, but there will always be winners and losers. I think it is probably time for us to try and look at the world in that way instead of this euphoria of everything works out.

Travis Hoium: Emily, you're in the room trying to pick stocks each month. Are you seeing more opportunities today, or are you seeing more risk?

Emily Flippen: I see a bit of both, to be honest with you, and it really depends on a company-by-company basis because I think, to lose points, AI can be an existential risk, and I know we saw a lot of that this earnings season. At the same time, there are great companies that are going, in my opinion, to come out the other side of this that the market is punishing, and I know we're going to talk about some of them later in the show. But the market just doesn't understand today how to price a lot of companies. In my opinion, that creates opportunities, but it does mean that you have to have the stomach for pretty intense levels of volatility because with great opportunity, does come great risk. In the market today, there's a lot of mispricing happening. Therefore, there's a lot of risk and a lot of confusion.

Travis Hoium: In a moment, we're going to talk about some of those potential opportunities. You're listening to Motley Fool and Jim's Investing. Welcome back to Motley Fool, Hidden Gems Investing. My big question for today is: are these non-AI stocks back? If we're seeing a pullback in AI stocks, does that mean some of the companies that the market was thinking were going to be disrupted by AI? Maybe that narrative not quite correct. A couple that caught my eye this week- maybe it's because I owned shares, but Duolingo jumped, I think, about 35% after their reported earnings. Their daily active user growth was phenomenal. This was a company that was supposed to know. People were just going to make their own language app on ChatGPT. Duolingo was supposed to be toast. Now they have more users than ever. The other one, we've been talking about agents for quite a while, Lou, but agents were supposed to be disruptive to almost everything, including Uber. Uber said that they've had about 500 orders for food with AI agents and about four orders for rides. One of those people said that it was a terrible experience and would just open the app next time. Are we in a place where we should really be starting to fish in this? You know what? Maybe AI isn't going to disrupt all of these companies pond.

Lou Whiteman: Well, first of all, I think we should note that yes, they both had great reactions. They're both still down big for the year. A lot of this is: don't read too much into one quarter or one reaction. They were left for dead to your point, and maybe they aren't dead. Duolingo is an interesting case, though, because, yes, they did very well. They get credit for creative disruption, but they are disrupting themselves. There is AI-related disruption. They're just not waiting for it to come. They said, We're going to focus on growing the user base, even if it means sacrificing profits. Indeed, daily active users is up big, but profits are down. We'll see if that's permanent or not. I think they're hoping it's not. But we are seeing even in this good result, we are seeing AI-related disruption here. Again, there is definitely a there with AI and they are definitely going to be changes to business models and changes to just maybe long term margins for some of these companies. To Duolingo credit, they're trying to be out in front of it. I think most of these companies are aware of it, so probably the narrative is overstated. But that doesn't necessarily mean they are going to be long-term winning investments, even if they are going to be survivors.

Travis Hoium: Emily, how do you think about finding opportunities that maybe the market thinks, Hey, this is really a disruption story. We're going to we went through this with Alphabet. It was only what 18 months ago. Search is dead. Turns out search wasn't dead. Maybe it's the growth.

Emily Flippen: Actually, for this past quarter.

Travis Hoium: Well, growth is slowing a little bit, but Lou, I think Lou hit it on the head with a lot of these companies. Everybody has read the disruption the book on Disruption that I'm blanking on right now, and everybody's trying to get out in front of it, and it seems like a lot of these companies are at least trying to figuring out a path forward. Maybe it isn't the same profitability as it used to be. But do you think that there are opportunities out there? I used two examples there that maybe you don't like, but where companies are trading for reasonably good valuations, and the story is, hey, they're toast in the future. But they've actually got pretty decent futures, and they're maybe not going to be disrupted by ChatGPT.

Emily Flippen: Yes, definitely. I agree with the premise there, Travis, which is that the market really tries to simplify this equation. They want to paint companies and industries with broad brushes. We saw that narrative earlier this year with the idea that software was dead, and a lot of great software companies came back and were like, actually, we're innovating with AI, and it's acting as a tailwind for our business. But that does not mean that every single software company has a place in the future when that future involves artificial intelligence. You have to figure out where that place is. In my opinion, this comes down to evaluating every individual company, understanding their approach to either how they're competing with AI or integrating AI, or, in a lot of times doing both. If you see a future where they work together well. I would not extrapolate someone like Uber who comes out and said, Well, we only had a handful of agentic rides last quarter. We only had a handful of agentic orders and say, Well, that's proof that AI isn't disrupting this business because I likely believe that the acceleration we're going to see with stuff like AI agents is going to happen aggressively and quickly. Uber himself actually said that they're getting intrigue and requests from AI assistants who want to integrate their app. In my opinion, that's a good thing for Uber. On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 27, 2026, X Financial (XYF -0.76%) announced a dramatic reduction in loan origination, or issuing new loans, as deteriorating credit quality forced a pivot toward balance sheet preservation. Shrinking loan volume reduces short-term fee income, but conserving cash helps the lender navigate an economic downturn safely. Three things management said stand out.

Management cut loan volume sharply to protect the balance sheet as early borrower default signals worsened. Choosing capital safety over origination volume protects long-term equity during market stress.

Customer acquisition spending plummeted as management pulled back on paid marketing channels. Focusing on internal channels keeps loan economics healthier while credit risks remain elevated across the industry.

The company expanded its equity asset ratio, which measures the proportion of assets backed by shareholder equity rather than debt, to 73%. High capital cushions provide defense against credit losses during industry downturns.

Macro headwinds and rising borrower delinquencies cloud near-term visibility, so management suspended numerical targets. High balance sheet equity, internal customer channels, and automated collection systems provide structural buffers while executive teams monitor early-stage borrower defaults and pricing discipline.

Navigating this credit cycle requires strict risk management until economic conditions stabilize. Management is anchoring its operational strategy on balance sheet protection to position the business for eventual recovery.

#2981. Grupo Financiero Galicia: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Falling NPLs and a shrinking efficiency gap leave investors weighing whether a 15% return target by 2028 is realistic.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:25PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Grupo Financiero Galicia ›

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 25, 2026, Grupo Financiero Galicia (GGAL +5.33%) reported net income of 229 billion Argentine pesos. Falling inflation compressed asset yields faster than deposit costs and reduced short-term profitability across the financial sector. Long-term investors must evaluate how the bank transitions from inflation-driven investment gains to loan-driven operating earnings. Three things management said stand out.

Asset quality improved during the period through stricter credit underwriting and disciplined collection efforts. Nonperforming loans, or NPLs, dropped to 7.8% of total loans. Loan loss provisions fell 12% sequentially to 509 billion Argentine pesos.

Management reduced operating expenses by 10% sequentially and 36% year over year to 731 billion Argentine pesos. Integration with HSBC Argentina helped lower administrative costs. Shares in Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.83%) rose by 5% at 1 p.m. today as the market continued to digest a couple of positive news developments for the company. The first is CEO Elon Musk's pledge to give every child in the U.S. two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from Musk personally. The second is the news that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) granted SpaceX the authority to deploy 1 million data centers in space.

The plan to gift shares is not only a huge display of generosity by Musk, but also creates significant goodwill around the company and strengthens public awareness of what SpaceX is doing in the space and AI industries.

Those aims are also strengthened by the FCC announcement, which clears a path for orbital data centers that SpaceX's management believes it could deploy as early as 2028. The idea is that the cost of orbital data centers will inevitably fall as rocket technology becomes more productive. Furthermore, orbital data centers don't face the power bottlenecks that many data centers do right now.

Orbital data centers address rising real estate, construction, and power costs and avoid the permitting issues that terrestrial data centers are increasingly facing. In addition, since Musk believes the price of compute will rise, revenue from orbital data centers may increase while costs decrease.

It's a key part of SpaceX's long-term growth program, and the FCC decision is a positive result. Still, there are many question marks around their ultimate deployment, not least the key question of how many years orbital data centers will actually be productive, given the likelihood that they won't be serviceable. Something to think about.

#2976. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2968. Rule Breaker Investing and "The Force For Good Project" With Sam Horn

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:44PM EST

Returning guest Sam Horn joins Motley Fool co-founder David Gardner to share the story behind her new book, The Force For Good Project, featuring 50 true stories of people adding remarkable value to our world today.

Bringing her signature storytelling style, Sam introduces us to extraordinary people whose lives invite us to ask: What do they have in common? What rules are they breaking? And what can we learn from their example?

Making the world better is something we can all take part in, through small acts of kindness, courage, and initiative.

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 11, 2026.

David Gardner: What does it mean to be a force for good? What happens when you seek out remarkable people who were quietly changing the world and ask them how they're doing it? What rules are they breaking? What new rules are they making, and what might we learn from their example? Perhaps, most importantly, what small things can you and I do starting today to make a difference? Well, my returning guest, author, and communication strategist, Sam Horn, has been asking these questions of some extraordinary people, and she's here to share their stories, their lessons, and a few surprises along the way. It's time to be a force for good, only on this week's Rule Breaker Investing.

Welcome back to Rule Breaker Investing. I hope my message to you last week came across loud and clear. I was advocating for investing a week ago over something that has a lot of buzz today, especially among younger people advocating for investing over sports betting, and also, some closing thoughts on how we make money in life. All that in less than 25 minutes. I hope last week's RBI podcast packed a punch for you. I know this week's will. My guest this week is someone many of you will remember from our Authors in August series last year. Sam Horn is a bestselling author, communication strategist, entrepreneur, and three-time TEDx speaker. She's the founder and CEO of the Intrigue Agency, and over the years has worked with organizations ranging from NASA and Intel to National Geographic and Accenture. She's written more than 10 books, including Tongue Fu!, Someday Is Not a Day in the Week, and Talking on Eggshells, which was the focus of our conversation last time. Sam has spent much of her career helping people communicate more effectively, resolve conflict, and turn good ideas into action, and now, she's turned her attention to something close to my own heart, and that's celebrating people who are making the world better. Her newest book, The Force for Good Project, Make a Difference Today and Every Day, brings together 50 true stories of people using their initiative, their creativity and agency to make a positive difference. Sam Horn, welcome back to Rule Breaker Investing.

Sam Horn: Thanks so much, David. I'm really looking forward to sharing some stories with your listeners.

David Gardner: Sam, in August of 2025, you were one of my Authors in August. As we spoke about your book, Talking on Eggshells, I was mentioning to you before we came online for this conversation just how I had recently gone out with a good friend of mine, a lifelong oncologist, somebody who's done untold good in his community, and he just talked about how much Talking on Eggshells was one of his favorite books ever. I'm thinking back to the conversation we had about that, and I asked you, at the time, this is August 2025, what was the most common power that we leave unused in everyday conversations, and I went back and checked it. You answered, "I really believe we can be a force for good." Now, here we are. It's November 2026. Your book, Force for Good, comes out in hardback next week. It is the very subject of this conversation. Sam, how did that idea grow into this project?

Sam Horn: I owe it all to Chris Anderson of TED. In 2025, I went to TED, and I think, David, you've been there, is that they have about 80 speakers, and the vast majority focus on the UN 12 sustainable goals, and it's inspiring. About 20 of them, David, were real doomsayers. They were sharing cautionary tales, and Chris read the room, and he could see the despair in the room, and he said, we're going to have a town hall on our final day, and if you have a message you want to share, go ahead, submit 90 seconds, and we're going to pick a few of you to be on the stage. Well, I knew I wanted to say something, and I didn't know what. I went to my room, and I kept thinking about what I had heard and the helplessness that many people felt, because there was nothing we could do about it, and you and I love quotes. Jose Ortega y Gasset said, "Tell me to what you pay attention, and I will tell you who you are." I thought, what am I going to give my attention to? Do we have time for the 90-second manifesto that poured out of me on that red dot?

David Gardner: Sam, you're really good at asking if we have time for stories. I've always said yes to every one of your stories, not just because they're all 60-90 seconds, although you must know that's compelling, yes. [LAUGHTER]

Sam Horn: Here we go. Red dot, TED, Vancouver. Our speakers have shown that there are two stories going on all around us all day, every day. There's the bad news, and there's the good news. The question is, which story will we feed? Which story will we lead? Will we rant and rail, and rave about what is wrong, or will we create, contribute to, and collaborate with what is right? I believe, when things go wrong, we don't have to go with them. We can Pablo Picasso our life. He said the purpose of life is to find our gifts. The meaning is to give them away. I think that what is ours to do on a daily basis is to create, collaborate with, and contribute to what's more right with the world by Pablo Picasso, our gifts, and if we do, we can be a force for good today and every day.

David Gardner: It's a beautiful phrase, and you've made it a big part of the title of your book, Force for Good Project. Sam, what does it mean to be a force for good? What qualifies someone as a force for good in your eyes?

Sam Horn: Now, we both love stories, David. Instead of telling what it means to be a force for good, we're going to go back to the beginning and show what it means. I am grateful to my parents, to a 300-pound pig, to my Palomino horse, and to a plane for teaching me, showing me what it means and what it looks like to be a force for good. I grew up in a really small town, Southern California, and we were in 4-H. One weekend, I thought, I'm going to plant a garden. Have you ever planted a garden?

David Gardner: No. But my wife has many times. My name is Gardner, ironically, yes.

Sam Horn: Well, then she knows that you spend all weekend. You till the soil, you have your rolls, you plant the seeds, you water it, etc. It's a painstaking, laborious, time-consuming thing, but I felt really good about it, went off to school. We came back home to our ranch. We came over the cattle guard, turned the corner, and have you heard the phrase happy as a pig in mud? [LAUGHTER]

Sam Horn: Well, my 300-pound pig, Ma Chow, was happy as a pig in mud, me not so much. I started wa-wa-waing about it, and my dad said that wailing and wallowing doesn't help. He said the question is, what are you going to do about it? I didn't know it, but that was the first lesson. What's a force for harm, wailing, wallowing? What's a force for good? What are we going to do about it? Now, my Palomino horse, Joe. Do you ride horses, David, by any chance?

David Gardner: Unfortunately, although my mother was an equestrian, I had a bad allergy to horses, Sam, and I still sneeze when I'm around them. I so wish I didn't, but I'm a little bit allergic to horses.

Sam Horn: Well, you would have been allergic to my Palomino Joe, because he had to piss. He trotted and he ran. He never walked, and he never loped. My friends would go, "Let's lope," and I'd go, "We're off to the races." [LAUGHTER] Now, here's the thing. I was 10-years-old riding this almost out-of-control horse. Did my parents worry about what might go wrong, and did they warn me about it? No. They expected things would go wrong, and they had faith that I would figure it out. It's another force for harm, force for good crossroads. Are we going to worry about what could go wrong? We're going to expect things to go wrong, and we'll figure it out when we get there. Now, one more thing. Now, I get to ask questions, because you said conversation, David.

David Gardner: I love it when you turn it around. This is one of the more fun interviews, it always is, Sam, because you're so engaging. What have you got for me?

David Gardner: Absolutely not. I have jumped out of a plane, though. [LAUGHTER]

Sam Horn: Well, see, we could go there in a moment. By the way, when we get there, we're going to circle back to it. I know you're taking notes. We're going to talk about why you jumping out of a plane wasn't just a dream or an adventure that, in its own way, I bet it served as a force for good. We're going to figure out how. Sound good?

Sam Horn: Back to the plane. I talked about this small valley that I lived in in Southern California, more horses than people. My dad was a private pilot, and now we had a little [inaudible] airport, a runway out in the middle of nowhere. We would get into his Cessna, and after he'd go through his checklist, he'd open his little window on the pilot side. That was unplanned, and I really appreciate let's close it out by me asking Sam, simply, what's your greatest hope for this book and for the people who encounter?

Sam Horn: Sartra said, "Freedom is what you do with what's been done to you." I think agency is what we do with what's been done to us and around us. Agency is the river that runs through this book. I think that on a daily basis, dozens of decisions, it's a force for harm, we can criticize, we can complain, we can create, we can contribute, we can get angry. We can use agency. What I hope for this book is that as people listen to these stories, that they ask in their life where they're tempted to go down that force for harm path, and use it as an excuse for why they're bitter, angry, and why this didn't work out, why they didn't get what they want. They shift over to agency, and they take responsibility just like with a 300-pound pig, just like a Palamino horse, just like a plane, no wah wah, wah. What am I going to do about it?

David Gardner: Sam, thank you for sharing some remarkable stories this week with us. The lessons that you've drawn from them, you're reminding us that being a force for good. You've said it, I'm going to say it again, is within everyone's reach. It's really those small acts of kindness, of courage and initiative, agency that can make a lasting difference. Sam, I'm grateful for your friendship and for what you've taught us today and for the good that you're bringing into this world, so I'm going to give you a resounding Fool on Sam Horn.

Sam Horn: Thank you, David. It was a joy.

#2965. AMD Shares Just Got Crushed on a Short Report. Why the Drop Is a Golden Buying Opportunity.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:44PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›

Following the takedown of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, a short-seller has decided to go after rival Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +4.56%)based on allegations that the company's chips are also being illegally directed to China. The report sent AMD shares plunging 20% in the two days following the short attack.

In its report, Hunterbrook Media, which is short AMD stock, claimed that the company is supplying support to its graphics processing units (GPUs) to banned Chinese companies. It alleged that U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems was continuing to get firmware updates that allowed it to use its chips on its servers. It also said that it gets around 20% of its revenue from customers in China and Hong Kong and that a Chinese partner finishes these chips.

However, the short-seller admitted that its own research didn't find any actual export-law violations. It added that it does not know how IEIT got AMD's code or whether it has a license for the firmware. So basically, it's accusing AMD of something with no proof, while saying it's actually not accusing it.

Overall, the short report is pretty flimsy; however, the market has been so on edge following the Nvidia news, and with artificial intelligence (AI) stocks in general struggling, Hunterbrook took advantage of the situation to try to make a quick buck.

For its part, AMD said that it "complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across [its] global operations." Otherwise, it did not engage with the short-seller regarding its accusations.

The chipmaker is allowed to sell its server central processing units (CPUs) in China, as well as certain older-generation GPUs to some Chinese customers, for which it has an export license.

The sell-off in AMD is a compelling entry point, in my view. The company is riding two huge waves with inference and agentic AI that should drive significant growth over the next few years.

AMD has built its new Helios system, which combines its GPUs and CPUs, around inference and agentic AI. Its chiplet GPU design, which can be packaged with more memory, is ideal for inference.

Meanwhile, the company has made some interesting acquisitions that could eventually push this further in future rack-scale solutions. This includes its purchase of predictive memory optimization company MEXT, and Taalas, which makes chips where specific AI models are embedded into them to speed up inference.

The launch of Helios comes at an opportune time, with Anthropic recently demonstrating that its Mythos Claude model could switch running models on Nvidia GPUs to AMD GPUs in just a few days. This could significantly weaken Nvidia's CUDA software moat at a time when AMD is just starting to ship Helios to large customers, including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, and Anthropic. With Helios costing nearly half of Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform per gigawatt, AMD has the potential to take significant share in the inference market over the next few years.

On top of that, the company is just starting to ride a huge wave with agentic AI for its server CPUs. AI agents require a significant amount of high-performance CPUs, which is a market AMD has been taking share in for years. The company's CPUs are helping run Meta's Muse AI agents, and it even has a foothold in Alphabet's lucrative tensor processing unit (TPU) architecture due to its strong security features, with its chips being chosen over Alphabet's own ARM-based CPUs.

Overall, AMD has a huge growth opportunity, and I'd use this pullback to buy the dip.

#2963. The Jordan Clarkson moment that shows why Knicks’ unique bench works so well

It was a guy who didn't play who served as a catalyst for the Knicks' most all-around win this year.

Coach Mike Brown used 12 players in the team's 121-102 win over the Cavs on Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden. Without OG Anunoby (calf strain) and Miles McBride (adductor tightness), it meant end-of-the-bench reserves got a rare chance to see some action.

Pacôme Dadiet had seven points in 14 minutes. Rookie Tyler Nickel, making his NBA debut (he has spent this year in the G-League), got nine minutes and had five points.

Mohamed Diawara got four minutes and chipped in three points. James Wiseman saw six minutes of action and helped seal the win with a few crucial rebounds late — he finished with six offensive boards.

Jordan Clarkson smiles before the Knicks' loss to the Pacers on Nov. 13, 2026, in Indianapolis. NBAE via Getty Images

Under Brown's anything-goes system, nobody is too far away from getting a chance. His love of experimentation, particularly early in the year, means players seemingly out of the rotation will get their opportunity to prove themselves at some point.

It has cultivated an egoless culture among the bench players, where they know the minutes will look different every night. It's a system of basketball socialism of sorts. But it's only possible because one member of that group set the tone for the rest.

"As a coach, you could want to do that, but you have to have others around you that will at least support it initially to see how it turns out," Brown said. "And a huge, huge, huge catalyst for that was Jordan Clarkson. Jordan Clarkson was the one, if you're talking about giving 100 percent out there to what allows me to do that, I think Jordan Clarkson gave me at least 90 percent of the opportunity to do it, because here's an accomplished veteran that could be in the rotation for almost any team out there, let alone a championship team, and I can literally play him six straight games and then sit him 10 straight games and he's gonna be the same dude every frickin' day.

"And he's gonna talk the same way to his teammates. Not 'can you believe what Mike Brown did?' Nah, he's gonna be the same dude, uplift the group, and then when I call his number again, he's gonna be ready to go.

"He's a guy that, even when he gets done playing, it's one of those things where you hope that he can just be a part of this organization in some way, shape or form until he doesn't want to be part of this organization. He's that type of person, in my opinion."

Clarkson missed Wednesday's game — the fourth straight he's been sidelined due to plantar fasciitis. But it was he who helped Dadiet — who has largely underwhelmed, now in his third year after the Knicks drafted him in the first round — deliver his best game as a pro.

"JC is always big on that, telling guys to stay ready," Jose Alvarado said. "He was in [Dadiet's] ear the whole shootaround [Wednesday morning]. Just telling everybody to stay ready because you never know when your name is called."

Pacome Dadiet rises up for a layup during the Knicks' win over the Cavaliers on Nov. 25, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Jason Szenes for NY Post

Alvarado himself had his best game of the year with 21 points in 19 minutes. But it wasn't long ago that he was out of the rotation, with Tyler Kolek having usurped him as the backup point guard.

But Brown has recently been experimenting with having Alvarado on the floor at the same time as Jalen Brunson, to allow Brunson to play off the ball more. And Brown has liked the results.

That has meant Alvarado is now cutting back into Kolek's minutes, despite Kolek continuing to play well. That could rub other players on other teams the wrong way — losing minutes despite not doing anything wrong, simply because the coach wants to try something new and see how it works out. For the bench players, nothing is set in stone, regardless of how you play.

This team embraces it, though. Brown compared the way this bench pulls for one another to the championship Spurs and Warriors teams he was an assistant on.

"We care about each other," Landry Shamet, currently the top dog of that bench unit, said. "We want to win for each other. We're willing to take on different roles and we know that we've got each other's back. If Jose's got it going and my minutes are shortened, awesome. And vice versa. All of us, Deuce [McBride] included in that, I would throw him in that as well, all of us kind of feel that way. That's really cool.

"I've been saying it, I've been a broken record about it, but you don't see that — that's very rare where no ego or ulterior motives get involved. That's something special that you want to be a part of."

Something special, sparked by a special personality in Clarkson.

#2959. A Thanksgiving thank you to the community that changed my life

**While this article mentions Phoenix Suns experiences, this piece is about the gratitude that comes with covering the team. So if you're looking for a piece analyzing the team's hot streak or Jalen Green's trade value, feel free to check out other content on Bright Side. **

It is well known in sports media circles that SB Nation sites serve as an incubation lab for young journalists. Being able to write about professional sports, and maybe even get paid to do so, helps so many people achieve their dreams much earlier than they expected while gaining real-world experience in what it's like to work in this profession full-time.

From covering the Super Bowl, the NBA Draft, or Hall of Fame ceremonies, what you put into your time at SB Nation is what you get out of it. But to earn those opportunities, you need people to trust you. And on this 2026 Thanksgiving, I'd like to thank the Bright Side community for helping me land my first full-time job in sports media.

First and foremost, thank you to every reader. Whether you're a frequent post commenter or this is the first Bright Side piece you've ever read, I appreciate you. Knowing there are always people to serve and that we get to share the unique access we have at the NBA Draft, playoff games, Summer League, and many other events keeps our purpose strong: serving passionate Suns fans.

To the late, great Dave King, Harrison Faigen, and John Voita, thank you for taking a chance on a 20-year-old and allowing me to fly out to Philadelphia to cover Kevin Durant and reigning MVP Joel Embiid. Your trust in me is what has allowed me to conduct one-on-one interviews with Khaman Maluach and Rasheer Fleming after they were drafted, sit down with Amar'e Stoudemire and Mike D'Antoni before their Hall of Fame inductions, and cover dozens of NBA events across the country. I've met so many of my media idols and learned so many lessons about the industry at a much younger age than I expected.

This is the wordy DM I sent to John Voita when I was 19, looking for a chance. ANY chance to write about the NBA.

The relationships, experiences, and lessons I've gained in the first few years of my media career helped me stay sane and confident during my job search. It took me about six months to find my first full-time job in sports media after graduating from Syracuse in May (where the voice of the Suns, Jon Bloom, also went!). While many people have had to wait much longer to find their first job, and plenty spend more than six months between gigs, the process still took a toll on me. But I knew that, thanks to my experience at Bright Side, I'd eventually end up somewhere doing what I love.

So, on a day centered around thankfulness, thank you, Bright Side, for helping me land my first full-time job in sports media. I'm now working as an on-air host at WeTheHobby, where I broadcast, livestream, and podcast about the latest happenings in the NBA collectibles space.

My Bright Side coverage is still the same as it's been since I joined the staff, but now I get to do it knowing that I'm a full-time sports media professional and that what I've learned from being a part of this community has played a major role in getting me here. I'm truly grateful.

Happy Thanksgiving, everyone! If only there were NBA games on today!
